26.title: Plain form + んです
26.meaning: Explains a cause, reason, or circumstance strongly.
26.explanation: Explains a cause, reason, or circumstance strongly. Spoken equivalent of ~のです. Three main uses: (1) んですか — guessing a reason and confirming it, or asking for an explanation; (2) んです — stating a reason as an answer; (3) んですが — introducing a topic before a request, invitation, or permission-seeking expression (softens the lead-in).

examples.jp: 渡辺さんは時々大阪弁を使いますね。大阪に住んでいたんですか。
examples.en: Ms. Watanabe, you sometimes speak Osaka dialect. Have you lived in Osaka?

examples.jp: どうして遅れたんですか。…バスが来なかったんです。
examples.en: Why were you late? — Because the bus didn't come.

examples.jp: 日本語で手紙を書いたんですが、ちょっと見ていただけませんか。
examples.en: I've written a letter in Japanese. Could you please check it for me?

26.note: Careful: んですか can sound like you're probing/surprised — overuse can come across as nosy. Don't use んです just to state a plain fact (わたしはマイク・ミラーです, not …なんです).
26.summary: んです softens or requests an explanation, framing a statement as following from something implied, observed, or already assumed — its three sentence-final forms each do a different conversational job.
26.details:
### The Three Jobs of 〜んです

| Form | Job | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **〜んですか** | Guessing a reason from what you see/hear, and confirming it — or asking someone to explain something surprising | 大阪に住んでいた**んですか**。 *(You lived in Osaka? — i.e., "so that explains the dialect")* |
| **〜んです** | Giving a reason as an answer, usually after being asked why | どうして遅れたんですか。…バスが来なかった**んです**。 |
| **〜んですが** | A softer lead-in before a request, invitation, or permission-seeking sentence | 手紙を書いたんです**が**、見ていただけませんか。 |

> **Common mistake**: んです is not a general-purpose politeness marker — don't attach it to a plain, context-free statement of fact. わたしはマイク・ミラーです is fine on its own; わたしはマイク・ミラー**なんです** sounds odd unless it's answering an implicit "who are you?" or explaining something. Overusing んですか can also come across as nosy or interrogating — reserve it for genuine curiosity about something you've noticed.

26.title: Vて-form + いただけませんか
26.structure: Vて-form + いただけませんか
26.meaning: A request expression, politer than ~てください.
26.explanation: A request expression, politer than ~てください.

examples.jp: いい先生を紹介していただけませんか。
examples.en: Would you please introduce a good teacher to me?

26.summary: てください < てもらえませんか / てくれませんか < てくださいませんか < ていただけませんか — this pattern sits near the top of the everyday politeness ladder for requests.
26.details:
### Where ていただけませんか Sits on the Request Ladder

| Expression | Politeness | Typical Use |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 〜てください | Plain, direct | Instructions, close relationships |
| 〜てくれませんか | Casual-polite | Friends, colleagues of similar status |
| 〜てくださいませんか (L41) | Polite | Slightly more formal request |
| **〜ていただけませんか** | Very polite | Asking a favor from someone you don't know well, or a status difference — the everyday "safe" polite request |
| 〜ていただけますでしょうか | Extremely formal | Business writing, customer service |

いい先生を紹介し**ていただけませんか**。 *(Would you please introduce a good teacher to me? — literally asking "could I receive the favor of your doing X")* — grammatically it's Vて-form + いただく (to receive, humbly) in its potential-negative-question form, which is what produces the softening effect.

26.title: Interrogative + Vた-form ら いいですか
26.structure: Interrogative + Vた-form ら いいですか
26.meaning: "What/when/where/which/how/who shall I ~?" — asking the listener for advice on what to do when you don't know.
26.explanation: "What/when/where/which/how/who shall I ~?" — asking the listener for advice on what to do when you don't know.

examples.jp: どこでカメラを買ったらいいですか。
examples.en: Where should I buy a camera?

26.summary: Asks for advice on what to do when you don't know — the conversational, たら-based counterpart to the more written-feeling ば-based version in Lesson 35.
26.details:
### たらいいですか vs ばいいですか

Both mean "what should I do?" and are interchangeable in most everyday conversation:

| Pattern | Feel | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Interrogative + Vたらいいですか** (here, L26) | Slightly more casual/conversational | どこでカメラを買っ**たらいいですか**。 |
| Interrogative + V conditional-ばいいですか (L35) | Slightly more neutral/written | どこでカメラを買**えばいいですか**。 |

Either works for asking "where/when/how/who should I ~?" when you genuinely don't know and want the listener's advice.

26.title: N(object)は 好きです/嫌いです・上手です/下手です・あります, etc.
26.structure: N(object)は 好きです/嫌いです・上手です/下手です・あります, etc.
26.meaning: Objects normally marked with が (or を) can be highlighted as the topic with は — same principle as Lessons 10 & 17 in Book I.
26.explanation: Objects normally marked with が (or を) can be highlighted as the topic with は — same principle as Lessons 10 & 17 in Book I.

examples.jp: 運動会に参加しますか。…いいえ。スポーツはあまり好きじゃないんです。
examples.en: Are you going to participate in the athletic meeting? — No, I don't like sports very much.

26.summary: Marking a normally-が/を object with は shifts it into the topic slot — usually to draw a contrast (I like X, but not Y) or because the object was already established as what's being discussed.
26.details:
### Objects Marked with は Instead of が/を

| Underlying pattern | With は (topicalized) | Nuance added |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| スポーツが好きです | スポーツ**は**好きです | Neutral topic-shift; often implies "as for sports (unlike other things)..." |
| 漢字がわかります | 漢字**は**わかりません | Contrast: "kanji I don't get (but maybe other things I do)" |
| コーヒーを飲みます | コーヒー**は**飲みません | "As for coffee, I don't drink it (implying something else I do drink)" |

スポーツはあまり好きじゃないんです is a good default example — は here doesn't just mark "sports" as the topic, it quietly invites the contrast "...though I might like other things." This is the same は-for-が/を substitution rule from Book I (Lessons 10 & 17): は always overrides が and を when a word is topicalized.

27.title: Potential Verbs
27.structure: Group I: -u→-e＋る／Group II: ＋られる／Group III: 来る→来られる、する→できる
27.meaning: Expresses the ability to do something, or the possibility that an action can happen, given the circumstances ("can do").
27.explanation:
All potential verbs conjugate as Group II verbs (dictionary form ends in -る). 
      Group I: change the final -u sound to the -e sound + る (かきます→かける, かいます→かえる) 
      Group II: ます-stem + られる (たべます→たべられる) 
      Group III: きます→こられます／します→できます 
      Note: わかる already contains the meaning of possibility, so it has no separate potential form.
27.summary: Expresses ability or situational possibility ('can do'). All potential verbs conjugate as Group II verbs.

27.title: Potential verb sentences — が instead of を
27.structure: Potential verb sentences — が instead of を
27.meaning: Potential verbs express states, not actions.
27.explanation: Potential verbs express states, not actions. Objects of transitive verbs, normally marked with を, are usually marked with が once the verb becomes potential (other particles are unaffected). Two uses: a person's ability to do something, or the possibility of an action in a given situation.

examples.jp: わたしは日本語が話せます。
examples.en: I can speak Japanese.

examples.jp: ミラーさんは漢字が読めます。／この銀行でドルが換えられます。
examples.en: Mr. Miller can read kanji. / You can change dollars at this bank.

27.summary: In potential sentences, the direct object switches from を to が because potential verbs describe a state of ability.
27.details:
### Particle Shift: を → が in Potential Sentences

Because potential verbs describe a **state** of capability rather than an active action, the direct object of a transitive verb is marked with **が** instead of **を**.

| Normal Action Sentence (`を`) | Potential State Sentence (`が`) | English Meaning |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 日本語**を**話します | 日本語**が**話せます | I can speak Japanese. |
| 漢字**を**読みます | 漢字**が**読めます | I can read Kanji. |
| 車**を**運転します | 車**が**運転できます | I can drive a car. |
| お酒**を**飲みます | お酒**が**飲めます | I can drink alcohol. |

> **Note on Other Particles:**
> Particles like **に**, **へ**, **で**, **から**, **まで** do NOT change:
> - 一人で病院**へ**行けます。 (I can go to the hospital alone.)
> - プール**で**泳げます。 (I can swim in the pool.)

27.title: 見えます・聞こえます
27.structure: 見えます・聞こえます
27.meaning: The potential form of 見ます is 見られます, and of 聞きます is 聞けます — but 見えます／聞こえます are separate verbs indicating that something comes into sight or a sound reaches the ears on its own, independent of the person's will.
27.explanation: The potential form of 見ます is 見られます, and of 聞きます is 聞けます — but 見えます／聞こえます are separate verbs indicating that something comes into sight or a sound reaches the ears on its own, independent of the person's will. The thing seen/heard is marked with が.

examples.jp: 新幹線から富士山が見えます。／ラジオの音が聞こえます。
examples.en: Mt. Fuji can be seen from the Shinkansen. / The sound of a radio can be heard.

27.summary: 見えます / 聞こえます describe natural sensory perception without intentional effort, whereas 見られます / 聞けます describe intentional ability or situational permission.
27.details:
### Comparison: Spontaneous Perception vs. Potential Ability Japanese distinguishes between what enters your eyes/ears naturally versus what you have the ability or opportunity to see/hear. | Category | Verb | Meaning & Nuance | Example Sentence | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Spontaneous Sight** | **見えます** (みえます) | Enters the field of vision naturally, without effort | 新幹線から富士山が**見えます**。
*(Mt. Fuji is visible from the Shinkansen.)* | | **Intentional Potential** | **見られます** (みられます) | Have the opportunity/ability/ticket to watch | 日本で歌舞伎が**見られます**。
*(You can watch Kabuki in Japan.)* | | **Spontaneous Sound** | **聞こえます** (きこえます) | Sound reaches the ears naturally | 鳥の声が**聞こえます**。
*(Bird song can be heard.)* | | **Intentional Potential** | **聞けます** (きけます) | Can listen intentionally (audio, radio, music) | インターネットで日本のラジオが**聞けます**。
*(You can listen to Japanese radio on the internet.)* |

27.title: できます
27.meaning: Here できます means "come into being," "be completed," "be made."
27.explanation: Here できます means "come into being," "be completed," "be made."

examples.jp: 駅の前に大きいスーパーができました。
examples.en: A big supermarket has been completed in front of the station.

27.summary: Here できます doesn't mean 'can do' — it means something has come into existence, been completed, or been made, a separate everyday meaning of the same verb.
27.details:
### The Two Faces of できます | Meaning | Example | | :--- | :--- | | **Potential** ("can do") — from する | 日本語が**できます**。 *(I can [do/speak] Japanese.)* | | **Come into being / be completed / be made** (a separate, non-potential verb) | 駅の前に大きいスーパーが**できました**。 *(A big supermarket has been built in front of the station.)*
もうすぐ晩ごはんが**できます**。 *(Dinner will be ready soon.)*
友達が**できました**。 *(I made a friend. — literally "a friend came into being")* | Context (usually an inanimate subject marked with が, describing something appearing/being finished) makes clear which meaning is intended — there's rarely real ambiguity in practice.

27.title: は / も / しか
27.meaning: は highlights a topic and replaces が/を, or follows other particles (で/に/へ/から/まで) — also used to make contrasts.
27.explanation: は highlights a topic and replaces が/を, or follows other particles (で/に/へ/から/まで) — also used to make contrasts. も means "also," replaces が/を (can be omitted before へ). しか is attached to nouns/quantifiers and is always used with a negative predicate — it replaces が/を, follows other particles, and highlights the word with a negative nuance (だけ has the same restrictive meaning, but positive nuance).

examples.jp: 京都へは行きますが、大阪へは行きません。
examples.en: I will go to Kyoto, but not to Osaka.

examples.jp: クララさんは英語が話せます。フランス語も話せます。
examples.en: Klara can speak English. She can also speak French.

examples.jp: ローマ字しか書けません。／ローマ字だけ書けます。
examples.en: I can't write anything but Roman letters. / I can only write Roman letters.

27.summary: は, も, and しか all replace が/を (or follow other particles) to add a nuance — contrast for は, addition for も, and a restrictive/negative nuance for しか (unlike だけ, which is restrictive but positive).
27.details:
### は／も／しか — Topic & Restriction Particles Compared

| Particle | Meaning | Replaces が/を? | Polarity | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **は** | Topic marker; often implies contrast | Yes | Either | 京都へ**は**行きますが、大阪へ**は**行きません。 |
| **も** | "Also" — adds a similar item | Yes (can drop before へ) | Either | フランス語**も**話せます。 |
| **しか** | "Nothing but / only" — restrictive, always negative-feeling | Yes | Must pair with a negative verb | ローマ字**しか**書けません。 |
| だけ (for comparison) | "Just / only" — restrictive, neutral/positive feeling | Yes | Either | ローマ字**だけ**書けます。 |

しか…ません and だけ…ます end up describing the same real-world fact ("I can only write Roman letters"), but しか frames it as a limitation/regret, while だけ frames it as a simple, neutral fact.

28.title: Vます-form + ながら V2
28.meaning: One person does two actions at the same time; the action expressed by V2 is the main, emphasized one.
28.explanation: One person does two actions at the same time; the action expressed by V2 is the main, emphasized one. Also used for two actions taking place over a period of time.

examples.jp: 音楽を聞きながら食事します。
examples.en: I listen to music while eating.

examples.jp: 働きながら日本語を勉強しています。
examples.en: I'm working while studying Japanese.

28.summary: ながら links two actions done by the same person at the same time, with the V2 action being the one that matters most — different from a plain て-form sequence, where one action finishes before the next starts.
28.details:
### ながら (Simultaneous) vs て-form (Sequential)

| Pattern | Timing | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Vます-stem ＋ ながら V2** | Both actions happen *at the same time*; V2 is the main action | 音楽を聞き**ながら**食事します。 *(I eat while listening to music — eating is the main activity.)* |
| V1て-form, V2 | V1 happens, *then* V2 happens | 音楽を聞い**て**、食事します。 *(I listen to music, then eat.)* |

ながら is also used more loosely for two long-running activities that overlap over a period of time, not just a single moment: 働きながら日本語を勉強しています (working while studying Japanese, as an ongoing lifestyle, not a single instant).

28.title: Vて-form + います (customary action)
28.explanation: Expresses an individual's habitual/customary action. A past habit uses Vて-form いました.

examples.jp: 毎朝ジョギングをしています。
examples.en: I jog every morning.

28.summary: Vて-form + います here isn't describing an action in progress right now — it describes a habit the person repeatedly does, a distinct use of て-form＋います from the progressive meaning learned earlier.
28.details:
### て-form ＋ います: Progressive vs. Habitual

| Use | Meaning | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **In progress** (earlier, more familiar use) | The action is happening right now | 今、走**っています**。 *(I'm running right now.)* |
| **Customary/habitual** (this point) | The person does this repeatedly as a habit | 毎朝ジョギングをし**ています**。 *(I jog every morning — an established habit, not necessarily happening right now.)* |

Context (adverbs like 毎朝, 毎週, いつも) usually signals the habitual reading. A past habit that no longer continues uses ていました: 学生のとき、毎朝ジョギングをしていました (I used to jog every morning back when I was a student).

28.title: plain form + し、〜
28.meaning: Links sentences from a certain viewpoint — often to list merits (or causes/reasons) of one subject.
28.explanation: Links sentences from a certain viewpoint — often to list merits (or causes/reasons) of one subject. Implies "furthermore / on top of that." Sometimes the conclusion is left unsaid when it's clear from context. Often paired with も to emphasize additional reasons. Note: this is different from 〜から, which does not imply other unstated reasons.

examples.jp: ワット先生は熱心だし、まじめだし、経験もあります。
examples.en: Professor Watt is earnest, diligent, and has experience.

examples.jp: 駅から近いし、車でも来られるし、この店はとても便利です。
examples.en: This shop is very convenient — it's near the station, and you can also come here by car.

28.summary: plain form ＋ し lists reasons or facts from one viewpoint, implying 'and furthermore' — unlike から, it leaves room for unstated additional reasons rather than presenting a single, complete cause.
28.details:
### し vs から: Listing Reasons

| Pattern | Implies | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **plain form ＋ し、〜（＋し）** | "X, and also Y, (and more reasons I won't even list)" — an open-ended, cumulative list, often building toward a conclusion | 熱心だ**し**、まじめだ**し**、経験もあります。 *(He's earnest, he's diligent, and he has experience — the reasons pile up.)* |
| **plain form ＋ から** | "Because X" — a single, specific, complete reason | 熱心だ**から**、いい先生です。 *(He's a good teacher because he's earnest — one clear cause.)* |

し is often paired with も (経験もあります) to emphasize "on top of everything else." Sometimes the conclusion is left unsaid entirely when it's obvious from context: 駅から近いし、車でも来られるし… (implying "...so it's convenient," without saying so).

28.title: それに
28.meaning: "In addition, moreover" — adds another similar fact or situation.
28.explanation: "In addition, moreover" — adds another similar fact or situation.

examples.jp: さくら大学は父が出た大学だし、いい先生も多いし、それに家から近いですから。
examples.en: Because it's my father's alma mater, there are many good teachers, and besides, it's near my house.

28.summary: それに adds one more similar fact on top of what was already said — 'and what's more' / 'besides.'
28.details:
### それに Among the Connecting Words

それに builds on a list of reasons or facts already stated, adding one more in the same direction — very often appearing right after a し-list (Lesson 28-3):

さくら大学は父が出た大学だ**し**、いい先生も多い**し**、**それに**家から近いですから。
*(It's my father's alma mater, there are many good teachers, and besides, it's near my house.)*

Compare with それで (28-5, cause→effect) and それでは/では (then, in that case) — それに specifically signals "here's one more point in the same direction," not a consequence or a new topic.

28.title: それで
28.meaning: A conjunction showing that what was said before is the reason/cause for what follows.
28.explanation: A conjunction showing that what was said before is the reason/cause for what follows.

examples.jp: このレストランは値段も安いし、おいしいんです。…それで人が多いんですね。
examples.en: The food here is inexpensive and tasty. — And that's why it's crowded.

28.summary: それで links a stated reason to its natural consequence — 'and so' / 'that's why.'
28.details:
### それで Among the Connecting Words

それで signals that what was just said is the cause, and what follows is the natural result — often used to react to someone else's explanation:

このレストランは値段も安いし、おいしいんです。…**それで**人が多いんですね。
*(The food here is cheap and tasty. — And that's why it's crowded, huh.)*

Compare それに (28-4, "and also," adding a similar fact) with それで (here, "and so," drawing out a consequence) — they're easy to mix up because both start with それ, but one adds, the other concludes.

28.title: よくこの喫茶店に来るんですか
28.structure: よくこの喫茶店に来るんですか
28.meaning: に (destination) is used instead of へ (direction) here.
28.explanation: に (destination) is used instead of へ (direction) here. Verbs like 行きます, 来ます, 帰ります, 出張します can take either 場所へ or 場所に.

examples.jp: よくこの喫茶店に来るんですか。
examples.en: Do you often come to this coffee shop?

examples.jp: 夏休みはうちに帰りますか。…いいえ、国に帰りません。
examples.en: Are you going home for summer vacation? — No, I'm not going back to my country.

28.summary: に and へ can often be swapped for verbs of motion, but they aren't identical: へ is strictly directional, while に also works for a fixed destination/point of arrival.
28.details:
### に vs へ with Verbs of Motion

Both particles are usable with 行きます、来ます、帰ります、出張します and similar verbs:

- よくこの喫茶店**に**来るんですか。
- よくこの喫茶店**へ**来るんですか。

へ emphasizes the *direction* of travel; に emphasizes the *destination point* itself. In casual conversation the two are largely interchangeable for these verbs, but に is required (へ cannot substitute) in constructions that aren't about physical direction at all, e.g. 銀行にお金を預けます (deposit money "at/into" the bank) — a distinction that becomes more important at N3.

29.title: N が Vて-form います (resulting state)
29.structure: N が Vて-form います (resulting state)
29.meaning: Expresses the state that results from an action, using mainly intransitive verbs that indicate an instantaneous act (壊れます, 消えます, 開きます, 込みます, etc.).
29.explanation: Expresses the state that results from an action, using mainly intransitive verbs that indicate an instantaneous act (壊れます, 消えます, 開きます, 込みます, etc.). The subject is marked with が. Contrast: 窓が割れました describes the event (it broke); 窓が割れています describes the resulting state (it is broken, right now). Past state uses Vて-form いました. When the subject is the known topic, は is used instead of が: このいすは壊れています。

examples.jp: 窓が割れています。／電気がついています。
examples.en: The window is broken. / The light is on.

examples.jp: けさは道が込んでいました。
examples.en: The road was crowded this morning.

29.summary: Intransitive verbs (自動詞) describe spontaneous states with が, while Transitive verbs (他動詞) describe deliberate actions with を.
29.details:
### Transitive (他動詞) vs. Intransitive (自動詞) Pairs

| Action / Actor (`他動詞 + を`) | Resulting State (`自動詞 + が + ています`) | English Meaning |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| ドア**を**開けます (あけます) | ドア**が**開いています (あいています) | Open the door / The door is open |
| ドア**を**閉めます (しめます) | ドア**が**閉まっています (しまっています) | Close the door / The door is closed |
| 電気**を**つけます | 電気**が**ついています | Turn on the light / The light is on |
| 電気**を**消します (けします) | 電気**が**消えています (きえています) | Turn off light / The light is off |
| コップ**を**割ります (わります) | コップ**が**割れています (われています) | Break a glass / The glass is broken |
| 車**を**止めます (とめます) | 車**が**止まっています (とまっています) | Park a car / The car is parked |
| ボタン**を**外します (はずします) | ボタン**が**外れています (はずれています) | Undo button / The button is undone |
| 鍵**を**掛けます (かけます) | 鍵**が**掛かっています (かかっています) | Lock key / The key is locked |

29.title: Vて-form + しまいました／しまいます
29.structure: Vて-form + しまいました／しまいます
29.meaning: Emphasizes that an action has been fully completed (often with もう or 全部).
29.explanation: Emphasizes that an action has been fully completed (often with もう or 全部). しまいました can also convey the speaker's embarrassment or regret about an unfortunate event (losing something, something breaking). The future form Vて-form しまいます expresses that the speaker will finish doing something.

examples.jp: シュミットさんが持って来たワインは全部飲んでしまいました。
examples.en: We drank all the wine that Mr. Schmidt brought.

examples.jp: パスポートをなくしてしまいました。
examples.en: I lost my passport. (regret)

examples.jp: 昼ごはんまでにレポートを書いてしまいます。
examples.en: I intend to finish writing the report by lunchtime.

29.summary: てしまいます marks that an action is fully, completely done — and depending on the verb and context, that completion can be framed as a relief, a regret, or just a plain statement of finishing something.
29.details:
### The Three Feelings of てしまいます

| Nuance | Example |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Complete finishing** (often with もう／全部) | ワインを全部飲ん**でしまいました**。 *(We drank all the wine — emphasizing "all of it, no more left.")* |
| **Regret / embarrassment** about something unfortunate | パスポートをなくし**てしまいました**。 *(I lost my passport — oops, and I feel bad about it.)* |
| **Future intention to finish something** (Vて-form しまいます, non-past) | 昼ごはんまでにレポートを書い**てしまいます**。 *(I intend to finish writing the report by lunchtime.)* |

In casual speech てしまう often contracts to ちゃう／じゃう (なくしちゃった for なくしてしまった) — worth recognizing in spoken Japanese even though the textbook form is what you'll produce.

29.title: ありました
29.meaning: Used to say the speaker has found something (not that it existed at some time in the past).
29.explanation: Used to say the speaker has found something (not that it existed at some time in the past).

examples.jp: ［かばんが］ありましたよ。
examples.en: I've found the bag!

29.summary: ありました here reports a discovery ('found it!'), not that something existed in the past — a subtle but important difference from the plain past tense of あります.
29.details:
### ありました: Discovery, Not Just Past Tense

- ［かばんが］**ありました**よ。 *("Here it is! / Found it!" — said the moment you spot the bag.)*

This is different from a plain statement that something existed at some point: 昔、ここに大きい木がありました (Long ago, there was a big tree here) is a genuine simple past. The "discovery" reading of ありました only applies when the speaker has just now located something they were looking for — context (searching for a lost item, then suddenly seeing it) is what signals this meaning.

29.title: どこかで／どこかに
29.meaning: Unlike へ in どこかへ or を in なにかを (which can be dropped), で in どこかで and に in どこかに cannot be omitted.
29.explanation: Unlike へ in どこかへ or を in なにかを (which can be dropped), で in どこかで and に in どこかに cannot be omitted.

examples.jp: どこかで財布をなくしてしまいました。／どこかに電話がありませんか。
examples.en: I lost my wallet somewhere. / Is there a pay phone somewhere nearby?

29.summary: どこかで and どこかに look similar to どこかへ／なにかを, but unlike those, the で and に here can never be dropped.
29.details:
### Particles That Can — and Can't — Be Omitted After か-Compounds

| Pattern | Particle droppable? | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| どこか**へ** | Yes, often dropped in casual speech | どこか（へ）行きましたか。 |
| なにか**を** | Yes, often dropped | なにか（を）食べましたか。 |
| どこか**で** | **No** | どこか**で**財布をなくしてしまいました。 |
| どこか**に** | **No** | どこか**に**電話がありませんか。 |

で marks the location *where an action happens* (lost my wallet somewhere) and に marks *existence* (is there a phone somewhere) — both of these particles carry essential grammatical information that へ and を don't, which is why they can't be casually dropped the way へ/を sometimes are.

30.title: N1に N2が Vて-form あります
30.structure: N1に N2が Vて-form あります
30.meaning: Indicates the state that results from an action intentionally done by somebody, using transitive verbs.
30.explanation: Indicates the state that results from an action intentionally done by somebody, using transitive verbs. N2は Vて-form あります is used when N2 is taken up as the topic. Often used with もう to show that some preparation has been done. Contrast with Vて-form います: 窓が閉まっています simply describes the window being closed (state), while 窓が閉めてあります implies somebody closed it on purpose. Most Vて-form います verbs are intransitive; verbs in Vて-form あります are transitive — many intransitive verbs have a transitive counterpart sharing part of the same kanji/reading (see 自動詞と他動詞, Main Textbook p.228).

examples.jp: 机の上にメモが置いてあります。
examples.en: There is a memo put on the desk.

examples.jp: 誕生日のプレゼントはもう買ってあります。／ホテルはもう予約してあります。
examples.en: I have already bought the present for her birthday. / I have already reserved a hotel.

30.summary: Nてあります describes the state left behind by someone's deliberate, purposeful action — contrast with Nています, which just describes a state with no implication that anyone did it on purpose.
30.details:
### てあります (Deliberate) vs ています (Just a State)

| Pattern | Verb type | Implies | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **N2が Vて-form います** | Intransitive | Just describes the resulting state, no mention of who caused it | 窓が閉まっ**ています**。 *(The window is closed — as a plain fact.)* |
| **N2が Vて-form あります** | Transitive | Someone deliberately did this, often in preparation | 窓が閉め**てあります**。 *(The window has been closed — by someone, on purpose.)* |

Most Vて-form います verbs are intransitive (自動詞); Vて-form あります always uses transitive verbs (他動詞), and many intransitive verbs have a transitive partner sharing part of the same kanji/reading (開く／開ける, 閉まる／閉める, つく／つける). もう often signals that a preparation has already been taken care of: ホテルはもう予約してあります (I've already reserved a hotel). When N2 is the established topic, は replaces が: プレゼントはもう買ってあります。

30.title: Vて-form おきます
30.meaning: Three related uses: (1) completing a necessary action by a given time, in preparation; (2) completing an action in readiness for the next use or step; (3) keeping the resultant state as it is.
30.explanation: Three related uses: (1) completing a necessary action by a given time, in preparation; (2) completing an action in readiness for the next use or step; (3) keeping the resultant state as it is. In daily conversation, 〜ておきます often contracts to 〜とく.

examples.jp: 旅行のまえに切符を買っておきます。
examples.en: I'll buy a ticket before the trip.

examples.jp: はさみを使ったら、元の所に戻しておいてください。
examples.en: When you finish using the scissors, put them back where they were.

examples.jp: あした会議がありますから、いすはこのままにしておいてください。
examples.en: Please leave the chairs as they are because a meeting will be held tomorrow.

30.summary: ておきます covers three related "do it now, for later" ideas: preparing ahead of time, tidying up after using something, and deliberately leaving a state as it is.
30.details:
### The Three Uses of ておきます

| Use | Example |
| :--- | :--- |
| **1. Prepare in advance** for a known future need | 旅行のまえに切符を買っ**ておきます**。 *(I'll buy a ticket before the trip.)* |
| **2. Restore/tidy up** after use, ready for next time | はさみを使ったら、元の所に戻し**ておいて**ください。 *(Put the scissors back where they were.)* |
| **3. Deliberately leave a state as-is** | いすはこのままにし**ておいて**ください。 *(Please leave the chairs as they are.)* |

In casual conversation, ておきます often contracts to とく／どく: 買っておく → 買っとく. This contraction is extremely common in spoken Japanese, so it's worth recognizing even though the full form is what you'll use in writing.

30.title: まだ V (affirmative)
30.meaning: "As yet" or "still" — indicates that the action or state is continuing.
30.explanation: "As yet" or "still" — indicates that the action or state is continuing.

examples.jp: まだ雨が降っています。
examples.en: It's still raining.

30.summary: まだ + affirmative verb means an action/state is still ongoing — the mirror image of まだ + Vていません (Lesson 31), which means something hasn't happened yet.
30.details:
### まだ, Two Ways

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **まだ ＋ affirmative** (here) | Something is *still* continuing | まだ雨が降っ**ています**。 *(It's still raining.)* |
| まだ ＋ Vて-form いません (L31) | Something *hasn't happened yet* | まだ書い**ていません**。 *(I haven't written it yet.)* |

Both use まだ, but the polarity of the verb completely flips the meaning — worth drilling side by side since the two are easy to mix up when speaking quickly.

30.title: それは〜
30.meaning: それ refers to what was stated just before by the other speaker — often followed by いいですね／おめでとうございます／いけませんね, etc.
30.explanation: それ refers to what was stated just before by the other speaker — often followed by いいですね／おめでとうございます／いけませんね, etc.

examples.jp: 来月結婚するんです。…それはおめでとうございます。
examples.en: I'm getting married next month. — Oh, congratulations!

examples.jp: きのう財布をなくしてしまったんです。…それはいけませんね。
examples.en: I lost my wallet yesterday. — Oh, that's too bad.

30.summary: それは〜 picks up what the other person just said and reacts to it — the reaction word that follows (いいですね／おめでとうございます／いけませんね, etc.) carries the actual sentiment.
30.details:
### それは〜 as a Conversational Reaction

それ refers back to the other speaker's preceding statement, and それは introduces the listener's reaction to it:

| Their statement | Your reaction |
| :--- | :--- |
| 来月結婚するんです。 | **それは**おめでとうございます。 |
| きのう財布をなくしてしまったんです。 | **それは**いけませんね。 |
| すごく忙しかったんです。 | **それは**大変でしたね。 |

This is a purely conversational pattern — you won't produce it out of context, only in response to something someone has just told you.

31.title: Volitional Form
31.structure: Group I: -u→-ō／Group II: ＋よう／Group III: 来る→来よう、する→しよう
31.meaning: The casual, plain-style equivalent of 〜ましょう — used to propose an action ("Let's...") or to express the speaker's own determination ("I will...").
31.explanation: Group I: replace the last sound of the ます-form with the equivalent お-line sound and attach う (かきます→かこう). Group II: attach よう to the ます-form (たべます→たべよう). Group III: します→しよう, きます→こよう.
31.summary: The casual equivalent of 〜ましょう, used for invitations ('Let's...') or expressing determination ('I will...').
31.details:

31.title: Plain-style use, and V volitional form + と思っています
31.structure: Plain-style use, and V volitional form + と思っています
31.meaning: In plain-style sentences the volitional form replaces 〜ましょう (か is still kept at the end even though the sentence is plain style).
31.explanation: In plain-style sentences the volitional form replaces 〜ましょう (か is still kept at the end even though the sentence is plain style). Vvolitional-form と思っています expresses what the speaker is thinking of doing; と思います is used right when the decision is made, while と思っています implies the decision was made some time ago. と思っています can also express a third person's will or intention.

examples.jp: 週末は海に行こうと思っています。
examples.en: I'm thinking of going to the beach at the weekend.

examples.jp: 彼は外国で働こうと思っています。
examples.en: He is thinking of working in a foreign country. (third person)

31.summary: In plain-style speech the volitional form itself replaces 〜ましょう (か still attaches at the end); Vvolitional-form ＋ と思っています reports a standing intention formed some time ago, contrasted with と思います for a decision made on the spot.
31.details:
### 意向形 in Plain Style, and と思います vs と思っています

- **Plain-style invitation**: 週末、映画を見に行**こうか**。 *(Shall we go see a movie this weekend? — か is kept even though everything else is plain.)*

| Pattern | Timing of the decision | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Vvolitional ＋ と思います** | Decided just now, in the moment of speaking | あ、コーヒーを飲もうと思います。 |
| **Vvolitional ＋ と思っています** | Decided some time ago; an ongoing intention | 週末は海に行こう**と思っています**。 |

と思っています can also describe a *third person's* intention (something only possible with the ている form, since you can't know someone else's momentary decision directly): 彼は外国で働こうと思っています。 (He is thinking of working abroad.)

31.title: Vdictionary form／Vない-form ない + つもりです
31.structure: Vdictionary form／Vない-form ない + つもりです
31.meaning: Expresses the speaker's intention of doing (or, with the ない-form, not doing) something.
31.explanation: Expresses the speaker's intention of doing (or, with the ない-form, not doing) something. Sounds more determined than V volitional form と思っています.

examples.jp: 国へ帰っても、柔道を続けるつもりです。／あしたからはたばこを吸わないつもりです。
examples.en: Even when I go back to my country, I'll continue with my judo. / I'm determined not to smoke from tomorrow.

31.summary: つもりです expresses a firmer, more determined intention than Vvolitional ＋ と思っています — on a scale from 'I'm thinking of...' to 'I'm resolved to...' to a firm scheduled 予定です.
31.details:
### Ranking Intention Expressions by Firmness

| Expression | Firmness | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Vvolitional-form ＋ と思っています (L31-2) | Considering, not fully decided | 続けようと思っています。 |
| **V dictionary／ない-form ない ＋ つもりです** (here) | Firm personal resolve/intention | 柔道を続ける**つもりです**。／たばこを吸わない**つもりです**。 |
| V dictionary form／Nの ＋ 予定です (L31-4) | An arranged, often external schedule, not just personal resolve | ドイツへ出張する**予定です**。 |

つもり can also take ない-form to express a determined *negative* intention (あしたからはたばこを吸わないつもりです — "I'm determined not to smoke from tomorrow"), which と思っています doesn't do nearly as naturally.

31.title: Vdictionary form／Nの + 予定です
31.meaning: Used to inform people of a schedule.
31.explanation: Used to inform people of a schedule.

examples.jp: 7月の終わりにドイツへ出張する予定です。
examples.en: I'm scheduled to go on a business trip to Germany at the end of July.

31.summary: 予定です announces a schedule or arrangement, as opposed to つもりです, which expresses personal intention/resolve — 予定 can apply even to things outside the speaker's own will.
31.details:
### 予定です: Schedules, Not Just Intentions

つもりです is about *your own resolve*; 予定です is about *what's arranged to happen*, which is why it also works for other people's or institutions' schedules, not just your own plans:

- 7月の終わりにドイツへ出張する**予定です**。 *(I'm scheduled to go on a business trip to Germany.)*
- 電車は9時に着く**予定です**。 *(The train is scheduled to arrive at 9.)* — つもり would be impossible here, since a train has no "intention."

Nの ＋ 予定です also works directly with a noun: 会議は来週の予定です (The meeting is scheduled for next week).

31.title: まだ Vて-form いません
31.structure: まだ Vて-form いません
31.meaning: Means that something has not taken place, or has not been done yet.
31.explanation: Means that something has not taken place, or has not been done yet.

examples.jp: レポートはもう書きましたか。…いいえ、まだ書いていません。
examples.en: Have you already written the report? — No, not yet.

31.summary: まだ ＋ Vて-form いません states something hasn't happened yet — the negative mirror of まだ ＋ affirmative (Lesson 30), which says something is still ongoing.
31.details:
See Lesson 30-3 for the full comparison of まだ + affirmative (something is *still* happening) vs まだ + ていません (something *hasn't happened yet*, here).

- レポートはもう書きましたか。…いいえ、**まだ書いていません**。 *(Have you written the report yet? — No, not yet.)*

Note that もう…ましたか ("have you already...?") is the natural question that triggers this pattern as an answer — もう and まだ work as a matched question/answer pair.

31.title: こ〜／そ〜 (in writing)
31.meaning: In writing, a demonstrative belonging to the そ-series usually refers back to a word or sentence mentioned before.
31.explanation: In writing, a demonstrative belonging to the そ-series usually refers back to a word or sentence mentioned before. Sometimes, however, a こ-series demonstrative is used instead, when the writer wants to describe something to the reader as if it existed right there.

examples.jp: きのう、駅で財布を拾った。その財布の中には、お金とカードが入っていた。
examples.en: Yesterday I found a wallet at the station. Inside that wallet were money and some cards.

examples.jp: この町には小さな図書館がある。この図書館は１００年前に建てられた。
examples.en: There is a small library in this town. This library was built 100 years ago. (こ used to bring the described thing vividly before the reader)

31.summary: In writing, そ-series demonstratives usually point back to something already mentioned — but a writer can deliberately switch to こ-series to make the described thing feel immediate and vivid to the reader.
31.details:
### こ〜 vs そ〜 in Written Japanese

| Series | Normal role in writing | Effect |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **そ〜 (それ／その／そこ, etc.)** | Refers back to something already mentioned in the text — the default choice | きのう、駅で財布を拾った。**その**財布の中には… |
| **こ〜 (これ／この／ここ, etc.)** | Occasionally substituted for そ〜 when the writer wants to describe something as if it were vividly present, right in front of the reader | この町には小さな図書館がある。**この**図書館は100年前に… |

This is purely a stylistic/rhetorical choice writers make (novels, essays, descriptive passages) — in ordinary conversation, そ〜 remains the default for referring back to something already said.

32.title: Vた-form／Vない-form ない + ほうがいいです
32.structure: Vた-form／Vない-form ない + ほうがいいです
32.meaning: Used to make suggestions or give advice.
32.explanation: Used to make suggestions or give advice. Depending on the situation this can sound like you're imposing your opinion, so consider the context carefully. Compare with 〜たらいい: that pattern is used for a simple suggestion with no explicit comparison, while 〜たほうがいい implies a comparison/choice between two things even if only one is mentioned.

examples.jp: 毎日運動したほうがいいです。
examples.en: It is good to do some exercise every day.

examples.jp: 熱があるんです。…じゃ、おふろに入らないほうがいいですよ。
examples.en: I have a fever. — So, you had better not take a bath.

32.summary: たほうがいいです gives advice framed as a comparison between two options (even if only one is stated) — stronger and more opinionated than a plain suggestion, so it's worth reading the room before using it.
32.details:
### たほうがいい vs a Plain Suggestion

| Pattern | Nuance |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Vた-form／ない-form ない ＋ ほうがいいです** (here) | Implies a comparison/choice between (at least) two options, even if the other option is left unstated — can sound like you're pushing your opinion | 毎日運動し**たほうがいいです**。 *(You'd better exercise every day — implying "rather than not exercising.")* |
| 〜たらいいです (softer alternative) | A plain suggestion, no implied comparison | 毎日運動し**たらいいです**。 *(It'd be good to exercise every day.)* |

Because ほうがいい carries that comparative, advice-giving weight, consider the social context carefully — with a boss or someone senior, a softer alternative may be more appropriate than sounding like you're telling them what to do.

32.title: plain form + でしょう
32.meaning: Expresses the speaker's inference from some information he/she has.
32.explanation: Expresses the speaker's inference from some information he/she has. When used in a question, it asks for the listener's inference.

examples.jp: あしたは雨が降るでしょう。
examples.en: It will rain tomorrow.

32.summary: でしょう states the speaker's own inference from available information; in a question, it instead asks for the listener's inference — different from a plain statement of fact.
32.details:
### でしょう: Inference, Statement or Question

| Form | Function | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| plain form ＋ でしょう。 | The speaker's own confident inference | あしたは雨が降る**でしょう**。 *(It will [probably] rain tomorrow — based on a forecast or the sky.)* |
| plain form ＋ でしょうか。 | Asking for the *listener's* inference/opinion, or a politer way of asking a question (see also L40-5) | あしたは晴れる**でしょうか**。 *(Do you think it'll be sunny tomorrow?)* |

でしょう is spoken with falling intonation for a statement, rising for a question — the same characters, different intonation and function.

32.title: plain form + かもしれません
32.structure: plain form + かもしれません
32.meaning: Also expresses the speaker's inference, meaning there's a possibility that something occurred/occurs/will occur — but with much lower certainty than 〜でしょう.
32.explanation: Also expresses the speaker's inference, meaning there's a possibility that something occurred/occurs/will occur — but with much lower certainty than 〜でしょう.

examples.jp: 約束の時間に間に合わないかもしれません。
examples.en: We might not be in time for the appointment.

32.summary: かもしれません expresses a possibility with much lower confidence than でしょう — the two sit at opposite ends of the certainty scale covered by きっと／たぶん／もしかしたら (Lesson 32-4).
32.details:
See **Lesson 32-4** for the full certainty ranking (きっと・たぶん・もしかしたら and their matching sentence endings).

- 約束の時間に間に合わない**かもしれません**。 *(We might not make it in time — a real possibility, but far from certain.)*

かもしれません pairs naturally with もしかしたら for extra emphasis on the low-certainty feel: もしかしたら3月に卒業できないかもしれません。

32.title: きっと／たぶん／もしかしたら
32.structure: きっと／たぶん／もしかしたら
32.meaning: Certainty adverbs, from most to least confident.
32.explanation: Certainty adverbs, from most to least confident. きっと = the speaker is quite certain (probability ranges from quite high up to the level of 〜でしょう). たぶん = less certain than きっと, often paired with 〜でしょう or 〜とおもいます. もしかしたら = used with 〜かもしれません, expresses a lower possibility of something occurring.

examples.jp: ミラーさんはきっと来ます。／たぶん来るでしょう。／もしかしたら3月に卒業できないかもしれません。
examples.en: Mr. Miller will surely come. / He'll probably come. / There's a chance I might not be able to graduate in March.

32.summary: きっと／たぶん／もしかしたら rank the speaker's certainty from highest to lowest, and each pairs with a specific sentence ending.
32.details:
### Adverbs of Certainty, Ranked

| Adverb | Certainty | Typical Pairing | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **きっと** | High — the speaker is quite confident | 〜でしょう／〜と思います／plain verb | ミラーさんは**きっと**来ます。 *(I'm sure Mr. Miller will come.)* |
| **たぶん** | Medium — likely, but less certain than きっと | 〜でしょう／〜と思います | **たぶん**来るでしょう。 *(He'll probably come.)* |
| **もしかしたら** | Low — just a possibility | 〜かもしれません | **もしかしたら**3月に卒業できないかもしれません。 *(There's a chance I might not graduate in March.)* |

> **Tip**: Think of these three adverbs and their sentence endings as fixed pairs — native speakers rarely mix a low-certainty adverb (もしかしたら) with a high-certainty ending (でしょう), or vice versa.

32.title: Quantifier + で
32.meaning: で added to a quantifier indicates the limit of a price, time, quantity, etc. necessary for a state, action, or event to be realized.
32.explanation: で added to a quantifier indicates the limit of a price, time, quantity, etc. necessary for a state, action, or event to be realized.

examples.jp: 駅まで30分で行けますか。／3万円でビデオが買えますか。
examples.en: Can I reach the station in thirty minutes? / Can I buy a video player for 30,000 yen?

32.summary: で attached to a quantifier marks the limit — the amount of time, money, etc. that's enough (or needed) for something to happen.
32.details:
### Quantifier ＋ で: Marking a Sufficient/Required Limit

- 駅まで30分**で**行けますか。 *(Can I get to the station within 30 minutes?)*
- 3万円**で**ビデオが買えますか。 *(Can I buy a video player for [as little/as much as] 30,000 yen?)*

で here marks the boundary condition — "with this much time/money, is X possible?" It commonly appears together with potential verbs (行けます, 買えます), since the question is almost always about whether something is achievable within that limit.

33.title: Imperative and prohibitive forms
33.structure: Imperative: Group I -u→-e／Group II ＋ろ／Group III 来る→来い、する→しろ ｜ Prohibitive: dictionary form ＋な
33.meaning: A direct, forceful way to command ("Do it!") or forbid ("Don't do it!") an action, used only in limited situations where full politeness isn't required or there's no time for it.
33.explanation: Imperative — Group I: change the last sound of the ます-form to the え-line sound (かきます→かけ); Group II: attach ろ to the ます-form (たべます→たべろ); Group III: します→しろ, きます→こい. Non-volitional verbs like わかる, できる, ある have no imperative form. Prohibitive: attach な to the dictionary form of any verb (使うな "don't use").
33.summary: Imperative (command: 'Do it!') and Prohibitive (prohibition: 'Don't do it!'). Strong expressions used in emergencies, traffic signs, and sports cheering.

33.title: Use of the imperative and prohibitive forms
33.structure: Use of the imperative and prohibitive forms
33.meaning: Both forms carry a strong, coercive nuance, so their use alone or at the end of a sentence is quite limited — mainly to: a senior speaking to a junior, or a father to his child; between male friends (よ is often added to soften it); when there isn't time to be polite (factory/emergency instructions); training/exercise commands; cheering at sporting events (ファイト！／負けるな！— usable by women too here); and traffic signs or slogans, where strong brevity is wanted (止まれ。／入るな。).
33.explanation: Both forms carry a strong, coercive nuance, so their use alone or at the end of a sentence is quite limited — mainly to: a senior speaking to a junior, or a father to his child; between male friends (よ is often added to soften it); when there isn't time to be polite (factory/emergency instructions); training/exercise commands; cheering at sporting events (ファイト！／負けるな！— usable by women too here); and traffic signs or slogans, where strong brevity is wanted (止まれ。／入るな。). Note: Vます-form + なさい is a gentler imperative used by parents to children or teachers to students — not used toward a senior.

examples.jp: 危ない！逃げろ！
examples.en: Watch out! Run!

examples.jp: 頑張れ！もう少しだ！
examples.en: Go for it! Almost there!

examples.jp: 早く起きなさい。学校に遅れるよ。
examples.en: Get up quickly. You'll be late for school. (a parent to a child — the gentler なさい form)

33.summary: The imperative/prohibitive forms are strong and coercive, so their use is limited to specific relationships and situations — a gentler なさい form exists for parent-to-child or teacher-to-student contexts.
33.details:
### When (and When Not) to Use the Bare Imperative/Prohibitive

| Context | Example |
| :--- | :--- |
| Senior → junior, or parent → child | 早く**しろ**。 |
| Between male friends (よ softens it) | 待て**よ**。 |
| No time to be polite (factory/emergency) | 逃げ**ろ**！ |
| Training/exercise commands | もっと**走れ**！ |
| Cheering at sports events (usable by anyone, including women) | ファイト！／負ける**な**！ |
| Traffic signs, slogans (brevity wanted) | 止まれ。／入る**な**。 |

> **Gentler alternative**: Vます-form ＋ なさい (早く起きなさい) is a softer command used by parents to children or teachers to students — appropriate in everyday family/school contexts where the bare imperative would feel too harsh, but still not used toward someone senior to the speaker.

33.title: 〜と読みます／〜と書いてあります
33.structure: 〜と読みます／〜と書いてあります
33.meaning: と here indicates the content, the same way as と in 〜といいます (Lesson 21).
33.explanation: と here indicates the content, the same way as と in 〜といいます (Lesson 21). Used to ask/state how a kanji is read, or what is written somewhere.

examples.jp: あの漢字は何と読むんですか。／あそこに「止まれ」と書いてあります。
examples.en: How do you read that kanji? / "Tomare" is written over there.

33.summary: と here marks quoted content — the same role と plays in 〜といいます (Lesson 21) — used to ask how a kanji is read, or to state what's written somewhere.
33.details:
### と for Content: 〜と読みます／〜と書いてあります

- あの漢字は何**と**読むんですか。 *(How do you read that kanji?)*
- あそこに「止まれ」**と**書いてあります。 *("Tomare" is written over there.)*

This is the same と you learned attaching to names in 〜といいます (この花は何といいますか — "What is this flower called?"). と always introduces the exact content — a name, a reading, or written text — regardless of which verb it's paired with.

33.title: XはYという意味です
33.explanation: Defines the meaning of X. どういう asks the meaning.

examples.jp: 「立入禁止」は入るなという意味です。
examples.en: "Tachiiri-Kinshi" means don't enter.

33.summary: XはYという意味です defines what X means; どういう意味ですか asks for that definition.
33.details:
### Asking For and Giving Definitions

- 「立入禁止」は入るな**という意味です**。 *("Tachiiri-Kinshi" means "don't enter.")*
- 「危険」って**どういう意味**ですか。 *(What does "kiken" mean?)*

という意味です is the natural way to explain unfamiliar vocabulary, signage, or kanji compounds to someone — an essential classroom/study phrase, since it lets you ask "what does that mean?" about anything you encounter.

33.title: "S" plain form + と言っていました
33.structure: "S" plain form + と言っていました
33.meaning: Used when conveying a third person's message, as opposed to 〜と言いました, which quotes a third person's exact words (Lesson 21).
33.explanation: Used when conveying a third person's message, as opposed to 〜と言いました, which quotes a third person's exact words (Lesson 21).

examples.jp: 田中さんは「あした休みます」と言っていました。＝田中さんはあした休むと言っていました。
examples.en: Mr. Tanaka said, "I will take a day off tomorrow." / Mr. Tanaka said that he would take a day off.

33.summary: plain form ＋ と言っていました reports someone's message in your own words (indirect quotation); 〜と言いました (Lesson 21) instead quotes their exact words.
33.details:
### Direct vs. Indirect Quotation

| Pattern | Type | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 「S」plain form ＋ と言いました (L21) | Direct — the exact words | 田中さんは「あした休みます」**と言いました**。 |
| **"S" plain form ＋ と言っていました** (here) | Indirect — the reported content, in plain form, regardless of how it was actually phrased | 田中さんはあした休む**と言っていました**。 |

Both sentences report the same fact, but the second treats it as conveyed information rather than a verbatim quote — です／ます endings inside the quote become plain form when reporting indirectly (休みます → 休む).

33.title: "S" plain form + と伝えていただけませんか
33.structure: "S" plain form + と伝えていただけませんか
33.meaning: Used to politely ask someone to convey a message on your behalf.
33.explanation: Used to politely ask someone to convey a message on your behalf.

examples.jp: すみませんが、渡辺さんにあしたのパーティーは6時からだと伝えていただけませんか。
examples.en: Could you please tell Ms. Watanabe that the party tomorrow will be from 6 o'clock?

33.summary: と伝えていただけませんか politely asks someone to pass a message along on your behalf — combining the quoting と with the polite request pattern ていただけませんか (Lesson 26).
33.details:
### Asking Someone to Relay a Message

すみませんが、渡辺さんにあしたのパーティーは6時からだ**と伝えていただけませんか**。
*(Could you please tell Ms. Watanabe that tomorrow's party starts at 6?)*

Breaking this down: 「6時からだ」＋ と (quoted content, L33-3) ＋ 伝える (to convey) ＋ Vて-form いただけませんか (polite request, L26-2). This combination is common when leaving messages through a third party — e.g. at a workplace, asking a colleague to pass something along to someone who isn't there.

34.title: V1 dictionary form／V1た-form／Nの + とおりに、V2
34.structure: V1 dictionary form／V1た-form／Nの + とおりに、V2
34.meaning: Means to copy exactly, in words or actions (V2), what one has heard, seen, read, or learnt (V1).
34.explanation: Means to copy exactly, in words or actions (V2), what one has heard, seen, read, or learnt (V1). The dictionary form is used when V1's action is going to be done from now on; the た-form is used when V1's action has already been done. Nのとおりに means an action is done in accordance with the manner shown by N.

examples.jp: わたしがやるとおりに、やってください。／説明書のとおりに、組み立てました。
examples.en: Please do as I do. / I assembled it according to the handbook.

34.summary: とおりに means to copy exactly what was seen, heard, read, or learned — the dictionary form is used before doing the action, the た-form after it's already been done, and Nのとおりに follows a noun directly.
34.details:
### とおりに: Copying an Example Exactly

| Form | Timing | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **V1 dictionary form ＋ とおりに** | The model (V1) is demonstrated *as* V2 happens | わたしがやる**とおりに**、やってください。 *(Do it the way I'm doing it, right now.)* |
| **V1た-form ＋ とおりに** | The model (V1) was already seen/heard/learned *before* V2 | 説明書に書いてあった**とおりに**、組み立てました。 *(I assembled it just as written in the manual.)* |
| **Nの ＋ とおりに** | Follows a manner shown by a noun | 地図の**とおりに**行けば、着きます。 *(If you go according to the map, you'll arrive.)* |

とおり literally means "the same as/following" — the choice between dictionary form and た-form purely tracks whether the model action happens simultaneously or was learned beforehand.

34.title: V1た-form／Nの + あとで、V2
34.meaning: V2 takes place after V1 (or N) has taken place.
34.explanation: V2 takes place after V1 (or N) has taken place. Compared with Vて-form から (similar meaning), 〜たあとで places more emphasis on the time context in which the two events happen.

examples.jp: 新しいのを買ったあとで、なくした時計が見つかりました。
examples.en: After I bought a new watch, I found the one I'd lost.

34.summary: V1たあとで places V2 after V1 has already happened — similar to Vて-form から, but with more emphasis on the time gap/context between the two events.
34.details:
### たあとで vs てから

| Pattern | Emphasis |
| :--- | :--- |
| **V1た-form／Nの ＋ あとで、V2** (here) | Emphasizes the *time context* — "in the period after V1" | 新しいのを買った**あとで**、なくした時計が見つかりました。 |
| Vて-form から、V2 (earlier lesson, similar meaning) | A more neutral, simple sequence — "V1, and then V2" | 新しいのを買っ**てから**、なくした時計が見つかりました。 |

Both are grammatically correct in most contexts; あとで leans slightly more toward "in the time that followed," while から is the more general-purpose sequential connector.

34.title: V1て-form／V1ない-form ないで + V2
34.structure: V1て-form／V1ない-form ないで + V2
34.meaning: V1 is an action or condition accompanying the action denoted by V2; both are done by the same person, and the pattern states whether V1 was done or not when V2 took place.
34.explanation: V1 is an action or condition accompanying the action denoted by V2; both are done by the same person, and the pattern states whether V1 was done or not when V2 took place.

examples.jp: しょうゆをつけて食べます。／しょうゆをつけないで食べます。
examples.en: We eat it with soy sauce. / We eat it without soy sauce.

34.summary: て-form/ないで-form + V2 states whether an accompanying action or condition (V1) was present or absent while V2 (done by the same person) took place.
34.details:
### With or Without: て-form vs ないで

| Form | Meaning | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **V1て-form ＋ V2** | V2 happens *with* V1 as an accompanying condition | しょうゆをつけ**て**食べます。 *(We eat it with soy sauce.)* |
| **V1ない-form ないで ＋ V2** | V2 happens *without* V1 | しょうゆをつけ**ないで**食べます。 *(We eat it without soy sauce.)* |

Both V1 and V2 must be actions of the *same person* — this is what distinguishes it from causal/contrastive patterns; here V1 simply describes the manner or accompanying state of V2, not a separate reason or event.

34.title: V1ない-form ないで、V2
34.meaning: Used when the speaker indicates a course of action chosen out of two alternative possibilities presented.
34.explanation: Used when the speaker indicates a course of action chosen out of two alternative possibilities presented.

examples.jp: 日曜日はどこも行かないで、うちでゆっくり休みます。
examples.en: Next Sunday I won't go anywhere. I will rest at home instead.

34.summary: ないで、V2 states a choice made between two possible courses of action — the speaker deliberately picked not doing V1 in favor of doing V2.
34.details:
### ないで as "Instead Of"

日曜日はどこも行**かないで**、うちでゆっくり休みます。
*(I won't go anywhere on Sunday — instead, I'll rest at home.)*

This overlaps closely with 34-3's ないで pattern (absence of V1 while V2 happens), but the emphasis here is specifically on choosing one alternative (resting at home) *over* another that was available or expected (going out). Context — usually a contrast implied between "going out" and "staying in" — signals this "instead of" reading.

35.title: Conditional ば-Form
35.structure: V: え-line＋ば／い-adj: 〜い→ければ／な-adj・N: だ→なら
35.meaning: Expresses a general condition, requirement, or logical consequence — "if/when X, then Y" — often used for rules, advice, and things that are reliably true.
35.explanation: How to make the conditional ば-form: Group I verbs change the final ます-stem sound to the え-line and add ば (押します→押せば); Group II attach れば to the ます-stem (見ます→見れば); Group III: きます→くれば, します→すれば. い-adjectives drop the final い and add ければ; な-adjectives and nouns drop な/だ and add なら.

examples.jp: 高い→高ければ　静か（な）→静かなら
examples.en: (if it's) expensive → たかければ　(if it's) quiet → 静かなら

35.summary: The 〜ば conditional expresses general conditions, requirements, or logical consequences ('if / when').

**よければ** | — | | **な-Adjectives** | `+ なら [ば]` | 暇 (ひま) | **暇なら [ば]** | — | | **Nouns** | `+ なら [ば]` | 雨 (あめ) | **雨なら [ば]** | — | --- ### Comparison of the 4 Conditionals | Conditional | Best Used For | Restriction | Example | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **〜と** | Natural results, machine operations, street directions | **No** requests/commands in 2nd clause | ボタンを押す**と**、切符が出ます。 | | **〜たら** | Most versatile conversational conditional; time sequence | Past fact or hypothetical | 雨が降っ**たら**、行きません。 | | **〜ば** | Logical conditions, advice, general rules | Formal / written nuance | 安けれ**ば**、買います。 | | **〜なら** | Contextual topic ('If you are talking about X...') | Follows nouns or plain forms | 温泉**なら**、白馬がいいですよ。 |

35.title: Conditional ば-form、〜
35.meaning: States the requirement needed for an event to occur, or the speaker's judgment about a situation.
35.explanation: States the requirement needed for an event to occur, or the speaker's judgment about a situation. When both clauses contain volition, the subject of both must be the same.

examples.jp: ボタンを押せば、窓が開きます。／いい天気なら、向こうに島が見えます。
examples.en: If you push the button, the window will open. / When the weather is good, you can see the island over there.

35.summary: Conditional ば states the requirement for something to happen, or the speaker's judgment about a hypothetical — when both clauses express volition, the subject of both parts must be the same person.
35.details:
### ば as Requirement / Judgment

- ボタンを**押せば**、窓が開きます。 *(If you push the button, the window opens — mechanical/reliable result.)*
- いい天気**なら**、向こうに島が見えます。 *(If the weather is good, you can see the island over there — a judgment/observation.)*

> **Same-subject rule**: When both halves express the speaker's own volition, the subject must match across both clauses — you can't say "If *I* do X, *you* will do Y" using ば when both parts are volitional. See Lesson 35-3 for the fuller restriction shared with 〜と.

35.title: 〜ば vs 〜と（L23）vs 〜たら（L25）
35.meaning: 〜と expresses an inevitable, predictable result and cannot be followed by the speaker's wishes, judgments, permission, hopes, or requests — the same restriction usually applies to 〜ば.
35.explanation: 〜と expresses an inevitable, predictable result and cannot be followed by the speaker's wishes, judgments, permission, hopes, or requests — the same restriction usually applies to 〜ば. 〜たら is the most flexible of the three: it can be followed by volitional expressions, but it's colloquial and less suited to formal writing.

examples.jp: 東京へ来たら、ぜひ連絡してください。（×東京へ来れば／×東京へ来ると、ぜひ連絡してください）
examples.en: Please contact me when you come to Tokyo. (only たら works, since the latter clause is a request)

35.summary: と and ば both resist being followed by the speaker's wishes, judgments, or requests — たら is the most flexible of the three, but that flexibility comes at the cost of sounding more colloquial.
35.details:
See **Lesson 35-1**'s details table for the full 4-way comparison (と／たら／ば／なら).

- 東京へ**来たら**、ぜひ連絡してください。 (○)
- 東京へ来れば／東京へ来ると、ぜひ連絡してください。 (×)

Because the second clause here is a *request*, only たら works — と and ば both reject volitional/request/permission endings (the same restriction applies to both), while たら freely accepts them. The tradeoff: たら is colloquial and less suited to formal writing, where と or ば often read better for the same neutral, non-volitional situations.

35.title: Nなら、〜
35.meaning: Used when the speaker picks up a topic the other person has just introduced, and gives related information about it.
35.explanation: Used when the speaker picks up a topic the other person has just introduced, and gives related information about it.

examples.jp: 温泉に行きたいんですが、どこかいい所ありませんか。…温泉なら、白馬がいいですよ。
examples.en: I want to go to a hot spring. Do you know a good place? …If you're talking hot springs, Hakuba is good.

35.summary: Nなら picks up a topic the other person just introduced and offers related information about it — distinct from the conditional なら attached to a full clause.
35.details:
### Topic-なら: Picking Up What Was Just Said

温泉に行きたいんですが、どこかいい所ありませんか。…**温泉なら**、白馬がいいですよ。
*(I want to go to a hot spring — know anywhere good? — If we're talking hot springs, Hakuba is good.)*

This なら isn't conditioning a hypothetical event — it's flagging "regarding the topic you just raised (温泉), here's my related information." It's a very natural, conversational way to respond helpfully to someone's question by picking up their own keyword.

35.title: Interrogative + V conditional-form + いいですか
35.structure: Interrogative + V conditional-form + いいですか
35.meaning: Asks for advice about the best course of action — equivalent to 〜たらいいですか, which you learned in Lesson 26.
35.explanation: Asks for advice about the best course of action — equivalent to 〜たらいいですか, which you learned in Lesson 26.

examples.jp: 本を借りたいんですが、どうすればいいですか。
examples.en: I'd like to borrow some books. What should I do?

35.summary: Interrogative + V conditional-ば + いいですか asks for advice on the best course of action — functionally the same question as たらいいですか (Lesson 26), just built on the ば-form instead.
35.details:
See **Lesson 26-3** for the side-by-side comparison of たらいいですか (slightly more conversational) vs ばいいですか (here, slightly more neutral/written) — both ask "what should I do?"

- 本を借りたいんですが、どう**すればいいですか**。 *(I'd like to borrow some books — what should I do?)*

35.title: V／い-adj／な-adj 条件形　V／い-adj／な-adj 辞書形＋ほど、〜
35.structure: V／い-adj／な-adj 条件形　V／い-adj／な-adj 辞書形＋ほど、〜
35.meaning: The same verb or adjective appears in both the ば-form half and the dictionary-form＋ほど half.
35.explanation: The same verb or adjective appears in both the ば-form half and the dictionary-form＋ほど half. Expresses that the degree described in the latter part increases (or decreases) as the degree in the former part changes — "the more..., the more...".

examples.jp: ビートルズの音楽は聞けば聞くほど好きになります。
examples.en: The more I listen to the Beatles' music, the more I like it.

35.summary: 条件形 + 辞書形ほど repeats the same verb/adjective in both halves to describe a degree that scales together — 'the more..., the more...'
35.details:
### 〜ば〜ほど: "The More..., the More..."

ビートルズの音楽は**聞けば聞くほど**好きになります。
*(The more I listen to the Beatles, the more I like them.)*

The same verb or adjective appears twice — once in the ば-conditional form, once in the dictionary form ＋ ほど — and the sentence describes how the degree in the second half tracks the degree in the first: 安ければ安いほどいいです (the cheaper, the better); 練習すればするほど上手になります (the more you practice, the better you get).

36.title: V potential-form／V ない-form ＋ ように、V2
36.structure: V potential-form／V ない-form ＋ ように、V2
36.explanation: Expresses a purpose or goal. Unlike 〜ために (Lesson 32), 〜ように is used when V1 is a non-volitional verb — a potential verb, or a verb of perception like わかる、見える、聞こえる — that can't itself express intention. V2 is the effort made toward that goal.

examples.jp: 速く泳げるように、毎日練習します。
examples.en: I practice every day so that I can swim fast.

36.summary: ように expresses purpose, but only with non-volitional verbs (potential forms, or perception verbs like わかる／見える／聞こえる) — ために (Lesson 42) is used instead when V1 itself expresses intention.
36.details:
### ように vs ために (see also Lesson 42-1)

| Pattern | V1 type | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **V-potential／V-ない-form ＋ ように、V2** (here) | Non-volitional — can't itself express intent (potential verbs, わかる, 見える, 聞こえる) | 速く**泳げるように**、毎日練習します。 *(I practice daily so that I can [become able to] swim fast.)* |
| V dictionary form／Nの ＋ ために、〜 (L42) | Volitional — an intentional goal | 自分の店を**持つために**、貯金しています。 *(I'm saving up in order to [intentionally] have my own shop.)* |

The test: can the verb before ように/ために itself express a deliberate intention? 泳げる ("can swim") can't — it's a state/ability, so ように is required. 店を持つ ("to have a shop," an intentional act) can — so ために is required there instead.

36.title: Vようになります／Vなくなります
36.structure: Vようになります／Vなくなります
36.meaning: Expresses a change of state — from unable to able, or the reverse — that has come about gradually or naturally, rather than through one deliberate act.
36.explanation: Expresses a change of state — from unable to able, or the reverse — that has come about gradually or naturally, rather than through one deliberate act.

examples.jp: 自転車に乗れるようになりました。／甘い物を食べなくなりました。
examples.en: I've become able to ride a bicycle. / I've stopped eating sweets.

36.summary: ようになります／なくなります describes a change of state that happened gradually or naturally over time — not through one single, deliberate act.
36.details:
### ようになります／なくなります: Gradual Change

- 自転車に**乗れるようになりました**。 *(I've become able to ride a bicycle — a gradual shift from "can't" to "can.")*
- 甘い物を**食べなくなりました**。 *(I've stopped eating sweets — a gradual shift, not necessarily one deliberate decision.)*

Compare with Lesson 36-3's ようにします, which is about ongoing *effort*, not a change that has already occurred. ようになります/なくなります describe the *result* of a change (whether or not it was deliberately pursued); ようにします describes the *ongoing attempt* to bring about a change.

36.title: Vようにします
36.meaning: Expresses the speaker's ongoing effort or resolution to make a habit of doing (or not doing) something.
36.explanation: Expresses the speaker's ongoing effort or resolution to make a habit of doing (or not doing) something.

examples.jp: できるだけ甘い物を食べないようにしています。
examples.en: I try not to eat sweets as much as possible.

36.summary: ようにします expresses the speaker's ongoing effort or resolution to make a habit of doing (or not doing) something — distinct from ようになります, which reports a change that has already taken hold.
36.details:
See **Lesson 36-2** for the direct comparison with ようになります/なくなります.

できるだけ甘い物を**食べないようにしています**。
*(I'm trying not to eat sweets as much as possible — an ongoing effort, with no claim that it has fully succeeded yet.)*

The ている form here (〜ようにしています rather than 〜ようにします) is the most common way to express this, since it frames the effort as a sustained, ongoing habit rather than a single decision.

36.title: 〜とか、〜とか
36.meaning: Lists a couple of examples out of other unstated possibilities — similar to や, but more casual, and often used with verbs/actions as well as nouns.
36.explanation: Lists a couple of examples out of other unstated possibilities — similar to や, but more casual, and often used with verbs/actions as well as nouns.

examples.jp: 踊るとか、泳ぐとか、いろいろします。
examples.en: I do various things, like dancing, swimming, and so on.

36.summary: とか、とか lists a couple of examples out of other unstated possibilities — like や, but more casual, and usable with verbs/actions as well as nouns.
36.details:
### とか vs や

| Pattern | Register | Can list actions/verbs? | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **〜とか、〜とか** (here) | Casual, conversational | Yes | **踊るとか**、**泳ぐとか**、いろいろします。 *(I do various things, like dancing, swimming, and so on.)* |
| 〜や〜（など） | Neutral | No — nouns only | ケーキ**や**クッキー**など**を食べます。 |

とか's flexibility with verbs (not just nouns) is what makes it distinct from や — it's the natural, casual way to list example activities in spoken Japanese.

37.title: Passive Verbs
37.structure: Group I: -u→-a＋れる／Group II: ＋られる／Group III: 来る→来られる、する→される
37.meaning: Describes an action done to the subject by someone else ("be praised," "be scolded") — including cases where the subject is inconvenienced or affected by another person's action.
37.explanation: All passive verbs conjugate as Group II verbs. Group I: change the final ます-stem sound to the あ-line and add れます (書きます→書かれます). Group II: drop ます and add られます (褒めます→褒められます). Group III: きます→こられます, します→されます.

examples.jp: 書く→書かれる　褒める→褒められる　来る→来られる　する→される
examples.en: write → be written　praise → be praised　come → (used when someone's coming affects me)　do → be done

37.summary: Passive voice describes actions received from another person (marked with に). All passive verbs conjugate as Group II verbs.
37.details:
### Passive Voice Conjugation (受身形の作り方) All passive verbs conjugate as **Group II verbs** (dictionary form ends in `-る`). | Verb Group | Conjugation Rule | Active Form | Passive Form | Meaning | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Group I (五段)** | Final `-u` sound → `-a sound + れる`
(`-imasu` → `-aremasu`) | 褒める (ほめます)
叱る (しかります)
頼む (たのみます)
踏む (ふみます) | **褒められる** (ほめられます)
**叱られる** (しかられます)
**頼まれる** (たのまれます)
**踏まれる** (ふまれます) | Be praised
Be scolded
Be requested
Be stepped on | | **Group II (一段)** | Drop `-る` → `+ られる` | 食べる (たべます)
見る (みます) | **食べられる** (たべられます)
**見られる** (みられます) | Be eaten
Be watched | | **Group III (不規則)** | Irregular | 来る (きます)
する (します) | **来られる** (こられます)
**される** (されます) | Be visited (suffering)
Be done | --- ### Core Sentence Patterns 1. **Direct Passive (Person A は Person B に V-passive)**: - わたしは先生**に褒められました**。 *(I was praised by the teacher.)* 2. **Suffering Passive on Object (Person A は Person B に Noun を V-passive)**: - わたしは弟**にパソコンを壊されました**。 *(My computer was broken by my younger brother.)* 3. **Invention / Creation (Object は Creator によって V-passive)**: - 電話はベル**によって発明されました**。 *(The telephone was invented by Bell.)*

37.title: N1（人）はN2（人）にVpassive
37.meaning: States another person's action from the point of view of the person it's directed at.
37.explanation: States another person's action from the point of view of the person it's directed at. That person (N1) becomes the topic, marked with は; the person who performs the action (N2) is marked with に. Something that moves (an animal, a car) can replace N2.

examples.jp: わたしは先生に褒められました。
examples.en: I was praised by my teacher.

37.summary: N1（affected person, topic）は N2（doer）に Vpassive states someone else's action from the point of view of the person it happens to; a moving thing (animal, vehicle) can fill the N2 slot too.
37.details:
わたしは先生**に**褒められました。 *(I was praised by my teacher.)*

N1 (は, the topic) is the person the action happens *to*; N2 (に) is the person who *performs* the action. This flips the perspective compared to the active sentence (先生はわたしを褒めました) — the passive puts the affected person front and center as the topic. N2 doesn't have to be a person: 犬に手をなめられました (I had my hand licked by a dog) works the same way.

37.title: N1（人）はN2（人）にN3をVpassive
37.meaning: Used when N2's action is directed at an object belonging to N1, and N1 feels troubled or annoyed by it.
37.explanation: Used when N2's action is directed at an object belonging to N1, and N1 feels troubled or annoyed by it. Note: the topic is N1 (the person affected), not N3 (the object) itself — わたしは弟にパソコンを壊されました is correct; わたしのパソコンは弟に壊されました is not.

examples.jp: わたしは弟にパソコンを壊されました。
examples.en: I had my personal computer broken by my brother.

37.summary: N1はN2にN3を Vpassive is used when N2's action affects an object belonging to N1, and N1 is troubled or annoyed by it — the topic stays N1 (the affected person), never N3 (the object).
37.details:
### The "Suffering Passive" on an Object

わたしは弟にパソコンを壊されました。 *(I had my computer broken by my brother — and I'm not happy about it.)*

> **Common mistake**: The topic must be N1 (the person inconvenienced), not N3 (the object itself).
> - ○ わたしは弟にパソコンを壊されました。
> - × わたしのパソコンは弟に壊されました。

This "suffering passive" construction inherently carries the nuance that the speaker was bothered or inconvenienced — it's not a neutral, purely descriptive statement the way Lesson 37-4's object-as-subject passive is.

37.title: N（物）が／はVpassive
37.meaning: Used when there's no need to mention who performs the action — the object itself becomes the subject of a passive verb, giving a purely objective, informational statement about things created, discovered, held, exported, and so on.
37.explanation: Used when there's no need to mention who performs the action — the object itself becomes the subject of a passive verb, giving a purely objective, informational statement about things created, discovered, held, exported, and so on.

examples.jp: フランスで昔の日本の絵が発見されました。
examples.en: An old Japanese picture was discovered in France.

37.summary: When there's no need to say who did it, the object itself becomes the subject of a passive verb — a purely objective, informational statement, unlike the affected-person passive in 37-2/37-3.
37.details:
### The "Objective/Informational" Passive

フランスで昔の日本の絵**が発見されました**。 *(An old Japanese picture was discovered in France.)*

Unlike 37-2/37-3 (which describe a person being affected, often negatively, by someone's action), this pattern is neutral and factual — used for things created, discovered, held, exported, published, and similar events, where *who* did it either isn't known or isn't the point. Typical in news reports and encyclopedic descriptions: 展覧会が開かれます、新しい本が出版されました, etc.

37.title: N1はN2（人）によってVpassive
37.meaning: When something is created, invented, or discovered, and the passive sentence identifies who did it, that person is marked with によって instead of に.
37.explanation: When something is created, invented, or discovered, and the passive sentence identifies who did it, that person is marked with によって instead of に. Used with verbs like かきます、はつめいします、はっけんします.

examples.jp: 「源氏物語」は紫式部によって書かれました。
examples.en: "The Tale of Genji" was written by Murasaki Shikibu.

37.summary: When identifying who created, invented, or discovered something, that person is marked with によって instead of the usual に.
37.details:
### によって: Marking the "Creator" in a Passive Sentence

「源氏物語」は紫式部**によって**書かれました。 *(The Tale of Genji was written by Murasaki Shikibu.)*

によって replaces に specifically in passive sentences about creation, invention, or discovery (書かれます、発明されます、発見されます) — it signals "by means of/through the work of," a slightly more formal, encyclopedic register than ordinary に. This によって does not extend to the "suffering passive" (37-3): you'd still use に for わたしは弟にパソコンを壊されました, not によって.

37.title: Nから／Nでつくります
37.meaning: When something is made from a raw material, the material is marked with から if it's no longer obvious to the eye once transformed.
37.explanation: When something is made from a raw material, the material is marked with から if it's no longer obvious to the eye once transformed. When the finished product still clearly shows what it's made of, で is used instead.

examples.jp: ビールは麦から造られます。／昔、日本の家は木で造られました。
examples.en: Beer is made from barley. / In the past, Japanese houses were made of wood.

37.summary: から marks a raw material that's no longer visibly recognizable in the finished product; で marks a material that's still visually obvious.
37.details:
### から vs で: Marking Raw Materials

| Particle | Condition | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **から** | The material is transformed beyond recognition | ビールは**麦から**造られます。 *(Beer is made from barley — you can't see the barley anymore.)* |
| **で** | The material is still visually apparent in the final product | 昔、日本の家は**木で**造られました。 *(Japanese houses were made of wood — you can clearly see it's wood.)* |

This distinction (recognizable vs. transformed) is the deciding factor, not the type of material itself — some materials could go either way depending on how visibly they survive into the finished product.

38.title: V plain form ＋ の
38.meaning: Attach the particle の to the plain form of a verb to turn the accompanying phrase into a noun phrase — "the act of doing...".
38.explanation: Attach the particle の to the plain form of a verb to turn the accompanying phrase into a noun phrase — "the act of doing...".

examples.jp: 絵を描くのは楽しいです。
examples.en: Drawing pictures is fun.

38.summary: Attaching の to a verb's plain form nominalizes the whole preceding phrase into 'the act of doing...' — the gateway to the rest of Lesson 38's patterns, which all build on this same nominalization.
38.details:
### の as a Nominalizer

絵を描く**の**は楽しいです。 *(Drawing pictures is fun.)*

の here isn't the possessive/explanatory の from earlier lessons — it turns an entire verb phrase (絵を描く, "to draw pictures") into a noun phrase ("the act of drawing pictures") that can then take any particle a normal noun could (は, が, を, etc.). Every other point in Lesson 38 is really just this same nominalization combined with a different following particle or predicate — see 38-2 through 38-7.

38.title: V dictionary formのは adjective です
38.structure: V dictionary formのは adjective です
38.meaning: Refers to an activity in general terms — playing or watching, depending on context.
38.explanation: Refers to an activity in general terms — playing or watching, depending on context. Adjectives frequently used here include むずかしい、やさしい、おもしろい、たのしい、きけん[な]、たいへん[な].

examples.jp: テニスをするのはおもしろいです。／テニスを見るのはおもしろいです。
examples.en: Playing tennis is fun. / Watching tennis is fun.

38.summary: V dictionary formのはadjective describes an activity in general terms — commonly paired with adjectives like むずかしい、おもしろい、たいへんだ. Context decides whether it is the doing or the watching being evaluated.
38.details:
テニスを**するのは**おもしろいです。／テニスを**見るのは**おもしろいです。
*(Playing tennis is fun. / Watching tennis is fun.)*

Common adjectives used with this pattern: むずかしい (difficult), やさしい (easy), おもしろい (interesting/fun), たのしい (enjoyable), 危険［な］(dangerous), 大変［な］(hard/tough). See Lesson 38-3 for the contrasting のが pattern, used with a different set of adjectives (likes/dislikes/skill).

38.title: V dictionary formのが adjective です
38.structure: V dictionary formのが adjective です
38.meaning: Used with adjectives describing likes, dislikes, and skills or abilities, such as すき[な]、きらい[な]、じょうず[な]、へた[な]、はやい、おそい.
38.explanation: Used with adjectives describing likes, dislikes, and skills or abilities, such as すき[な]、きらい[な]、じょうず[な]、へた[な]、はやい、おそい.

examples.jp: わたしは花を育てるのが好きです。
examples.en: I like growing flowers.

38.summary: V dictionary formのがadjective is used specifically with adjectives of liking, disliking, and skill/ability — a different adjective set from the のは pattern in 38-2.
38.details:
### のは vs のが: Which Adjectives Go With Which

| Particle | Typical adjectives | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **のは** (L38-2) | むずかしい、おもしろい、たのしい、危険［な］、大変［な］ — general evaluation | テニスをするのは**おもしろい**です。 |
| **のが** (here) | 好き［な］、嫌い［な］、上手［な］、下手［な］、はやい、おそい — likes/dislikes/skill | 花を育てるのが**好き**です。 |

The split isn't arbitrary — it mirrors the same が/は pattern you already know from N(object)は好きです (Lesson 26-4): liking/skill adjectives naturally pair with が, and that carries over here when the "object" being liked is a nominalized verb phrase instead of a plain noun.
