38.title: V dictionary formのを忘れました
38.structure: V dictionary formのを忘れました
38.meaning: "Forgot to do..." — the nominalized action becomes the object of 忘れます.
38.explanation: "Forgot to do..." — the nominalized action becomes the object of 忘れます.

examples.jp: 車の窓を閉めるのを忘れました。
examples.en: I forgot to close the car window (and left the car with it open).

38.summary: V dictionary formのを忘れました means 'forgot to do...' — the nominalized action becomes the direct object of 忘れます, distinct from forgetting a physical object.
38.details:
### 忘れました: Forgetting to Do vs. Forgetting an Object

- 車の窓を**閉めるのを**忘れました。 *(I forgot to close the car window — forgot to do an action.)*
- 傘を**忘れました**。 *(I forgot my umbrella — left behind a physical object.)*

The のを nominalization is what turns 忘れます from "forgot [a thing]" into "forgot to [do something]" — without の, 忘れました can only take a plain noun object.

38.title: V plain formのを知っていますか
38.structure: V plain formのを知っていますか
38.meaning: Asks whether the listener knows about what's described in the の-clause.
38.explanation: Asks whether the listener knows about what's described in the の-clause. [Note] しりませんでした is used when the listener has just gained the information from the question itself; しりません is used when they still have no information at all.

examples.jp: 鈴木さんが来月結婚するのを知っていますか。…いいえ、知りませんでした。
examples.en: Do you know Mr. Suzuki is getting married next month? …No, I didn't (until now).

38.summary: V plain formのを知っていますか asks whether the listener already knows about the fact described in the の-clause — with a careful distinction between しりません and しりませんでした depending on when the information was learned.
38.details:
### しりません vs しりませんでした

鈴木さんが来月結婚するの**を知っていますか**。…いいえ、**知りませんでした**。
*(Do you know Mr. Suzuki is getting married next month? — No, I didn't [until just now].)*

| Response | When used |
| :--- | :--- |
| **知りませんでした** | The listener just learned the fact *from this very question* — "I didn't know [until you told me]" |
| **知りません** | The listener still has no information at all, even after hearing the question | 

This distinction is subtle but important: しりませんでした acknowledges that the question itself supplied new information, while しりません would sound like the question didn't register at all.

38.title: V／い-adj／な-adj plain form（な-adjだ→な）のはNです
38.structure: V／い-adj／な-adj plain form（な-adjだ→な）のはNです
38.meaning: A thing, person, or place is nominalized with の and taken up as the topic of the sentence; the speaker gives related information about it in the latter half.
38.explanation: A thing, person, or place is nominalized with の and taken up as the topic of the sentence; the speaker gives related information about it in the latter half.

examples.jp: 娘が生まれたのは北海道の小さな町です。
examples.en: My daughter's birthplace is a small town in Hokkaido.

38.summary: A thing, person, or place is nominalized with の and made the topic; the rest of the sentence gives related information about it — effectively an identification/definition sentence built on a nominalized clause.
38.details:
娘が生まれた**のは**北海道の小さな町です。
*(My daughter's birthplace is a small town in Hokkaido — literally, "the place where my daughter was born is...")*

This pattern is often used to answer "when/where/who" questions with a full clause instead of a single noun: 会議があるのは3時からです (The meeting starting time is from 3 o'clock), 手伝ってくれたのは田中さんです (The one who helped me was Mr. Tanaka).

38.title: 〜ときも／〜ときや／〜ときの／〜ときに, etc.
38.structure: 〜ときも／〜ときや／〜ときの／〜ときに, etc.
38.meaning: Various particles can attach to 〜とき (Lesson 23), because とき is itself a noun.
38.explanation: Various particles can attach to 〜とき (Lesson 23), because とき is itself a noun.

examples.jp: 生まれたときから、ずっと大阪に住んでいます。
examples.en: I have been living in Osaka since I was born.

38.summary: Because とき is itself a noun (Lesson 23), it can take any particle a noun normally would — ときも、ときや、ときの、ときに, and more, each adding its own nuance.
38.details:
### とき + Particle Combinations

| Combination | Nuance | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **ときから** | "Since the time when..." | 生まれた**ときから**、大阪に住んでいます。 |
| **ときも** | "Even at the time when..." | 忙しい**ときも**、運動します。 |
| **ときの** | Modifies a following noun | 子どもの**ときの**写真 *(a photo from childhood)* |
| **ときに** | Emphasizes a specific point in time | 出かける**ときに**、かぎをかけます。 |

Since とき behaves exactly like any other noun, this list isn't exhaustive — any particle that combines meaningfully with a point in time can attach the same way.

39.title: Vて-form／Vない-form なくて／い-adj（〜い→くて）／な-adj［な］→で、〜
39.structure: Vて-form／Vない-form なくて／い-adj（〜い→くて）／な-adj［な］→で、〜
39.meaning: The first part gives a cause, the second its consequence.
39.explanation: The first part gives a cause, the second its consequence. Unlike 〜から (Lesson 9), this pattern has real constraints: the latter clause must describe an involuntary feeling or state (びっくりする、あんしんする、こまる、さびしい、うれしい、ざんねんだ, potential verbs, verbs of state) rather than volition — if the latter clause expresses will, orders, invitations, or requests, から must be used instead. The two events are also sequential: the first happens, then the second follows.

examples.jp: ニュースを聞いて、びっくりしました。／事故があって、バスが遅れてしまいました。
examples.en: I was surprised to hear the news. / Because of an accident, the bus was delayed.

39.summary: て-form/くて/で causal linking requires the second clause to describe an involuntary feeling or state — if the second clause expresses will, an order, an invitation, or a request, から must be used instead.
39.details:
### The Volition Restriction on て-form-as-Cause

| Allowed after て-form-cause | Not allowed |
| :--- | :--- |
| Involuntary feelings/states: びっくりする、あんしんする、こまる、うれしい、ざんねんだ、potential verbs | Volition, orders, invitations, requests |

ニュースを**聞いて**、びっくりしました。 (○ — びっくりする is an involuntary reaction)
ニュースを聞いて、家に帰りましょう。 (× — 帰りましょう is volitional; から is required instead: ニュースを聞いた**から**、家に帰りましょう。)

Also note the sequential nature: the first event happens, and the feeling/state *follows* it — unlike から, which can express a reason with no particular time-ordering implied. See Lesson 39-2 (Nで) and 39-3 (ので) for related cause-expressions with their own restrictions — Lesson 39-3's details table gives a full 4-way comparison.

39.title: Nで
39.meaning: The particle で learned here indicates a cause.
39.explanation: The particle で learned here indicates a cause. It's used with nouns describing natural phenomena or events, such as じこ、じしん、かじ — and like the pattern above, cannot be followed by expressions of volition.

examples.jp: 地震でビルが倒れました。
examples.en: Because of the earthquake, a building collapsed.

39.summary: で attached to a noun of natural phenomena or events (じこ、じしん、かじ) marks a cause — like the て-form pattern above, this で also can't be followed by an expression of volition.
39.details:
地震**で**ビルが倒れました。 *(Because of the earthquake, a building collapsed.)*

This で is reserved for nouns describing events/phenomena (事故、地震、火事、台風, etc.) rather than any general noun — see Lesson 39-3's comparison table for how this fits alongside から／ので／て-form as ways to express cause.

39.title: V／い-adj／な-adj plain form（な-adjだ→な）ので、〜
39.structure: V／い-adj／な-adj plain form（な-adjだ→な）ので、〜
39.meaning: Like 〜から, indicates a cause or reason, but 〜ので presents the cause-and-effect relationship more objectively, as a natural course of events, softening the impact on the listener — often used to gently ask permission or make an excuse.
39.explanation: Like 〜から, indicates a cause or reason, but 〜ので presents the cause-and-effect relationship more objectively, as a natural course of events, softening the impact on the listener — often used to gently ask permission or make an excuse. Unlike から, it's not used with imperative or prohibitive forms.

examples.jp: 日本語がわからないので、英語で話していただけませんか。
examples.en: I don't understand Japanese, so would you please speak in English?

39.summary: から, ので, and Vて-form/で all express cause-and-effect, but differ in objectivity, softness, and what kind of clause can follow.
39.details:
### Comparing Cause/Reason Expressions

| Pattern | Nuance | Can Follow with Volition/Request/Command? | Typical Use |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **plain form ＋ から** | Straightforward, speaker's own subjective reason | Yes | Everyday reasoning, giving your own opinion: 熱があるから、休みます。 |
| **plain form ／ Nな ＋ ので** | Softer, more objective — presents the reason as a natural fact rather than personal opinion | No (not with imperative/prohibitive; awkward with strong volition) | Polite requests, excuses, formal writing: 熱があるので、休ませていただけませんか。 |
| **Vて-form／Vなくて／い-adj くて／な-adj で ＋ 〜** | The two events are sequential (first happens, then the feeling/state follows); the second clause must be an involuntary feeling or state | No | Reacting emotionally to news or an event: ニュースを聞いて、びっくりしました。 |
| **N ＋ で** | Cause is a noun describing an event or natural phenomenon (事故, 地震, 火事) | No | Formal/news-style cause statements: 地震でビルが倒れました。 |

> **Quick check**: If the sentence ends in a command, request, invitation, or strong declaration of will, use **から** — never ので, で, or the て-form pattern above.

39.title: とちゅうで
39.meaning: とちゅう means "during" or "on the way", and follows a verb's dictionary form or Nの.
39.explanation: とちゅう means "during" or "on the way", and follows a verb's dictionary form or Nの.

examples.jp: 来る途中で事故があって、バスが遅れてしまったんです。
examples.en: On my way here, there was an accident and the bus was delayed.

39.summary: とちゅう means 'during' or 'on the way,' and attaches after a verb's dictionary form or Nの.
39.details:
来る**途中で**事故があって、バスが遅れてしまったんです。
*(On my way here, there was an accident and the bus was delayed.)*

Common combinations: V dictionary formとちゅうで (来る途中で, 帰る途中で), Nのとちゅうで (仕事のとちゅうで, "in the middle of work"). とちゅう literally breaks down as "mid-way" — useful for describing something that happened partway through a journey or activity, before it was completed.

40.title: Interrogative + V／い-adj／な-adj（だ→N/a）plain form ＋ か、〜
40.structure: Interrogative + V／い-adj／な-adj（だ→N/a）plain form ＋ か、〜
40.meaning: A question containing an interrogative word (何、いつ、どこ, etc.) is embedded as a component of a larger sentence.
40.explanation: A question containing an interrogative word (何、いつ、どこ, etc.) is embedded as a component of a larger sentence.

examples.jp: JL107便は何時に到着するか、調べてください。
examples.en: Please check what time flight JL107 will arrive.

40.summary: A question containing an interrogative word (何、いつ、どこ, etc.) can be embedded, plain form + か, as a component inside a larger sentence.
40.details:
JL107便は**何時に到着するか**、調べてください。
*(Please check what time flight JL107 will arrive.)*

The embedded question (何時に到着するか) functions as the object of 調べてください — this lets you report or ask about a question indirectly, rather than as a standalone direct question. Compare with Lesson 40-2 (かどうか), used when the embedded question has no interrogative word at all.

40.title: V／い-adj／な-adj（だ→N/a）plain form ＋ かどうか、〜
40.structure: V／い-adj／な-adj（だ→N/a）plain form ＋ かどうか、〜
40.meaning: A question without an interrogative word is embedded using plain form ＋ かどうか, "whether or not".
40.explanation: A question without an interrogative word is embedded using plain form ＋ かどうか, "whether or not". Note: まちがいがあるかどうか is not used when the speaker wants to confirm there are no mistakes — まちがいがないかどうか is used instead.

examples.jp: 忘年会に出席するかどうか、20日までに返事をください。
examples.en: Please answer by the 20th whether or not you'll attend the year-end party.

40.summary: かどうか embeds a yes/no question (one without an interrogative word) — 'whether or not' — with one important negative-polarity trap around まちがいがある vs ない.
40.details:
### かどうか: Embedding a Yes/No Question

忘年会に出席する**かどうか**、20日までに返事をください。
*(Please answer by the 20th whether or not you'll attend the year-end party.)*

> **Careful**: When you want to confirm there are *no* mistakes, まちがいが**ない**かどうか is used — not まちがいがあるかどうか. The polarity of the embedded verb should match what you're actually checking for, not just default to the affirmative.

40.title: Vて-form みます
40.meaning: Shows that the action denoted by the verb is a trial — done to see what happens or to find out.
40.explanation: Shows that the action denoted by the verb is a trial — done to see what happens or to find out.

examples.jp: このズボンをはいてみてもいいですか。
examples.en: May I try on this pair of trousers?

40.summary: て-form + みます frames an action as a trial — done to see what happens or find something out, not a routine or permanent action.
40.details:
このズボンを**はいてみても**いいですか。 *(May I try on this pair of trousers?)*

てみます always implies "as an experiment/to find out," which is why it combines so naturally with permission-seeking てもいいですか — you're asking to try something out, not asking to do it as a settled fact. Other examples: 食べてみます (try eating it), 聞いてみます (try asking).

40.title: い-adj（〜い→さ）
40.meaning: Change the final い of an い-adjective to さ, and you can transform the adjective into a noun — typically used for measurements.
40.explanation: Change the final い of an い-adjective to さ, and you can transform the adjective into a noun — typically used for measurements.

examples.jp: 高い→高さ　長い→長さ　速い→速さ
examples.en: high → height　long → length　fast → speed

40.summary: Changing an い-adjective's final い to さ turns the adjective into a noun — typically used for measurements and other nominalized qualities.
40.details:
### い-adjective → noun via さ

高い → **高さ** (height)　長い → **長さ** (length)　速い → **速さ** (speed)　重い → **重さ** (weight)

This nominalization is especially common with measurement adjectives, letting you ask about or state a quantity: この橋の長さはどのぐらいですか (How long is this bridge?). Not every い-adjective nominalizes this naturally in everyday use, but the pattern itself (〜い → 〜さ) is fully productive/regular.

40.title: 〜でしょうか
40.meaning: 〜でしょうか, which is used to ask a question whose answer the listener might be uncertain of, is also used to ask a question the listener is sure to be able to answer.
40.explanation: 〜でしょうか, which is used to ask a question whose answer the listener might be uncertain of, is also used to ask a question the listener is sure to be able to answer. In that case it's simply a more euphemistic, polite way of asking.

examples.jp: ハンスは学校でどうでしょうか。
examples.en: How is Hans doing at school? (a politer way of asking どうですか)

40.summary: でしょうか isn't only used when the listener might be uncertain — it's also a simple, more euphemistic, politer way of asking an ordinary question.
40.details:
ハンスは学校で**どうでしょうか**。 *(How is Hans doing at school? — a politer way of asking どうですか。)*

The literal meaning ("I wonder...") softens what would otherwise be a plain, direct question — even when the speaker fully expects the listener to know the answer easily. This overlaps with the question-form use covered in Lesson 32-2 (でしょうか asking for the listener's inference) — here the "inference" framing is just a politeness device, not genuine uncertainty about whether the listener knows.

41.title: N1にN2をやります
41.meaning: When the receiver is of lower social status, or an animal or plant, やります is normally used.
41.explanation: When the receiver is of lower social status, or an animal or plant, やります is normally used. However, when the receiver is a person, あげます is often preferred in current Japanese.

examples.jp: わたしは犬にえさをやりました。
examples.en: I gave some food to the dog.

41.summary: Giving and receiving verbs form a three-way system (やる／あげる／さしあげる for giving down/across/up, もらう／いただく for receiving, くれる／くださる for someone giving to you) that shifts depending on relative social status.
41.details:
### Giving & Receiving Verbs, by Social Direction

| Direction | Casual / Lower Receiver | Neutral (Equal Status) | Higher Status Involved |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **I give to someone** | あげる (person) ／ **やる** (animal, plant, or clearly lower status) | あげる | **さしあげる** (to someone of higher status) |
| **Someone gives to me** | くれる | くれる | **くださる** (from someone of higher status) |
| **I receive from someone** | もらう | もらう | **いただく** (from someone of higher status) |

- **やります** is reserved for animals, plants, or people clearly below the speaker (younger siblings, one's own children) — for a person of equal or higher status, あげます is generally preferred even in casual speech nowadays.
- **いただきます** and **くださいます** apply the same logic to the giving/receiving of actions (Vて-form ＋ やります／いただきます／くださいます), not just objects.
- Status also determines the direction of who is elevated: くださる elevates the giver; いただく and さしあげる elevate the *other party*, not the speaker (the speaker's own action stays humble).

41.title: N1にN2をいただきます
41.meaning: When the speaker receives a thing from a person of higher social status, いただきます is used instead of もらいます.
41.explanation: When the speaker receives a thing from a person of higher social status, いただきます is used instead of もらいます.

examples.jp: わたしは部長にお土産をいただきました。
examples.en: I received a souvenir from the general manager.

41.summary: いただきます replaces もらいます when receiving something from someone of higher social status — the humble-language partner of もらいます, elevating the giver rather than the speaker.
41.details:
See **Lesson 41-1**'s details table for the full giving/receiving system by social direction.

わたしは部長に**お土産をいただきました**。 *(I received a souvenir from the general manager.)*

いただきます is grammatically identical to もらいます in structure (N1にN2をもらいます／いただきます) — only the verb itself changes to signal that N2 (the giver) outranks the speaker.

41.title: ［わたしに］N2をくださいます
41.meaning: When a person of higher social status gives the speaker something, くださいます is used instead of くれます.
41.explanation: When a person of higher social status gives the speaker something, くださいます is used instead of くれます. It's also used when the receiver is a member of the speaker's family.

examples.jp: 部長がわたしにお土産をくださいました。
examples.en: The general manager gave me a souvenir.

41.summary: くださいます replaces くれます when a person of higher status gives the speaker something — also used when the giver is a family member of the speaker.
41.details:
部長がわたしに**お土産をくださいました**。 *(The general manager gave me a souvenir.)*

Note the direction: くださいます elevates the *giver* (unlike いただきます/さしあげます, which elevate the *other party* while keeping the speaker's own action humble). See Lesson 41-1's table for how くださいます sits within the full giving/receiving system.

41.title: Vて-form やります／いただきます／くださいます
41.structure: Vて-form やります／いただきます／くださいます
41.meaning: These same status-based expressions extend to the giving and receiving of actions, not just things.
41.explanation: These same status-based expressions extend to the giving and receiving of actions, not just things. [Note] Like てあげます (Lesson 24), てさしあげます may sound arrogant if used to address a person of higher status directly — so it's best avoided in direct address.

examples.jp: わたしは息子に紙飛行機を作ってやりました。／部長の奥さんは［わたしに］お茶を教えてくださいました。
examples.en: I made a paper airplane for my son. / The general manager's wife taught me the tea ceremony.

41.summary: The same status-based logic (やる／あげる／さしあげる, もらう／いただく, くれる／くださる) extends from giving/receiving objects to giving/receiving actions, via Vて-form.
41.details:
### Extending Giving/Receiving Verbs to Actions

- わたしは息子に紙飛行機を**作ってやりました**。 *(I made a paper airplane for my son.)*
- 部長の奥さんは［わたしに］お茶を**教えてくださいました**。 *(The manager's wife taught me the tea ceremony.)*

> **Careful with てさしあげます**: Like てあげます, using てさしあげます to address a person of higher status *directly* can sound presumptuous or arrogant — even though it's grammatically "more polite," it implies you're doing them a favor, which can come across as condescending. It's safer to avoid in direct address and use it only when talking *about* having done something for a superior in a neutral, reporting context.

41.title: Vて-form くださいませんか
41.structure: Vて-form くださいませんか
41.meaning: A polite expression of request — though less polite than ていただけませんか, which you learned in Lesson 26.
41.explanation: A polite expression of request — though less polite than ていただけませんか, which you learned in Lesson 26.

examples.jp: コピー機の使い方を教えてくださいませんか。
examples.en: Will you kindly show me how to use the photocopier?

41.summary: てくださいませんか is a polite request — one notch below ていただけませんか (Lesson 26) on the everyday politeness ladder for requests.
41.details:
See **Lesson 26-2**'s request-ladder table (てください → てくれませんか → てくださいませんか → ていただけませんか → ていただけますでしょうか).

コピー機の使い方を**教えてくださいませんか**。 *(Will you kindly show me how to use the photocopier?)*

てくださいませんか literally asks "won't you give me [the favor of doing this]?" — polite and appropriate for most everyday requests to someone you don't know well, though ていただけませんか is used when you want to sound even more deferential.

41.title: NにV
41.meaning: This particle に means "as a token of" or "in memory of".
41.explanation: This particle に means "as a token of" or "in memory of".

examples.jp: 田中さんが結婚のお祝いにこのお皿をくださいました。
examples.en: Mr. Tanaka gave this plate as my wedding gift.

41.summary: This に means 'as a token of' or 'in memory of' — marking the occasion or purpose behind a gift.
41.details:
田中さんが結婚のお祝い**に**このお皿をくださいました。
*(Mr. Tanaka gave this plate as my wedding gift.)*

This is a distinct use of に from location/time/indirect-object marking — here it attaches to an occasion noun (お祝い, "celebration/congratulation") to explain the reason or occasion behind a gift: 誕生日にプレゼントをもらいました (I got a present for my birthday), 記念にこの本をあげます (I'll give you this book as a memento).

42.title: V dictionary form／Nの ＋ ために、〜
42.structure: V dictionary form／Nの ＋ ために、〜
42.meaning: Indicates a purpose — "in order to V" or "for the sake of N".
42.explanation: Indicates a purpose — "in order to V" or "for the sake of N". [Note] 〜ように (Lesson 36) also expresses purpose, but is used with verbs that don't contain volition, while 〜ために is used with verbs that do. 自分の店を持つために、貯金しています (I intentionally set up the goal of having my own shop) contrasts with 自分の店が持てるように、貯金しています (my objective is a state I might attain, "being able to have a shop").

examples.jp: 自分の店を持つために、貯金しています。／家族のために、うちを建てます。
examples.en: I am saving money in order to have my own shop. / I will build a house for my family.

42.summary: ために means 'in order to' or 'for the sake of' — see Lesson 36-1 for the crucial distinction from ように, which is used instead when the verb before it can't itself express intention.
42.details:
See **Lesson 36-1**'s details for the full ように vs ために comparison.

- 自分の店を**持つために**、貯金しています。 *(I am saving money in order to have my own shop — an intentional goal.)*
- 家族の**ために**、うちを建てます。 *(I will build a house for my family — "for the sake of.")*

> **Contrast**: 自分の店を持つために、貯金しています (I intentionally set the goal of having my own shop) vs 自分の店が持てるように、貯金しています (my aim is a state I might attain — "being able to have a shop," using the non-volitional potential form). Same real-world situation, different framing of intention vs. attainable state.

42.title: V dictionary formの／N ＋ に、〜
42.meaning: As you learned in Lesson 38, V dictionary formの can be used as a noun phrase.
42.explanation: As you learned in Lesson 38, V dictionary formの can be used as a noun phrase. V dictionary formのに and Nに are followed by expressions like つかう、いい、べんりだ、やくにたつ、［じかんが］かかる, etc., and indicate a purpose or use.

examples.jp: このはさみは花を切るのに使います。／このかばんは大きくて、旅行に便利です。
examples.en: This pair of scissors is used to cut flowers. / This bag is big and convenient for trips.

42.summary: V dictionary formのに and Nに (built on the nominalization from Lesson 38) indicate purpose or use, typically followed by つかう、いい、べんりだ、やくにたつ、［じかんが］かかる and similar expressions.
42.details:
このはさみは**花を切るのに**使います。 *(This pair of scissors is used to cut flowers.)*
このかばんは大きくて、**旅行に**便利です。 *(This bag is big and convenient for trips.)*

Compare with Lesson 42-1's ために: に here doesn't express "in order to do X," but rather "for the purpose/use of X" — it typically pairs with a fixed small set of predicates (使う, いい, 便利だ, 役に立つ, 時間がかかる) describing how well-suited something is to a purpose, rather than describing someone's intentional goal.

42.title: Quantifier ＋ は
42.meaning: When attached to a quantifier, the particle は indicates the minimum amount the speaker estimates is required or necessary.
42.explanation: When attached to a quantifier, the particle は indicates the minimum amount the speaker estimates is required or necessary.

examples.jp: 日本では結婚式をするのに200万円は要ります。
examples.en: In Japan you need at least 2 million yen to hold a wedding.

42.summary: Quantifier + は indicates a minimum — the least amount the speaker estimates is required or necessary.
42.details:
日本では結婚式をするのに200万円**は**要ります。
*(In Japan you need at least 2 million yen to hold a wedding.)*

は here signals "at the very least, this much" — the actual amount could well be more, but the speaker is stating a floor. Compare with Lesson 42-4's quantifier + も, which instead signals that an amount is surprisingly *large*, not a minimum estimate.

42.title: Quantifier ＋ も
42.meaning: When attached to a quantifier, the particle も indicates that the speaker thinks the amount mentioned is a lot.
42.explanation: When attached to a quantifier, the particle も indicates that the speaker thinks the amount mentioned is a lot.

examples.jp: 駅まで行くのに2時間もかかりました。
examples.en: It took as long as two hours to get to the station.

42.summary: Quantifier + も indicates that the speaker views the stated amount as a lot — the counterpart to Lesson 42-3's は, which instead marks a minimum estimate.
42.details:
駅まで行くのに**2時間も**かかりました。
*(It took as long as two hours to get to the station — the speaker is emphasizing how much that is.)*

| Particle | Signals | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Quantifier ＋ は (L42-3) | "At least this much" (a minimum) | 200万円**は**要ります。 |
| **Quantifier ＋ も** (here) | "As much/many as this!" (surprisingly large) | 2時間**も**かかりました。 |

Both particles attach directly to a number+counter phrase and add the speaker's subjective framing on top of the plain fact.

43.title: Vます-form／い-adj（〜い）／な-adj［な］＋ そうです
43.structure: Vます-form／い-adj（〜い）／な-adj［な］＋ そうです
43.meaning: When the look of a thing leads you to a supposition, you can state that supposition with this pattern.
43.explanation: When the look of a thing leads you to a supposition, you can state that supposition with this pattern. The supposition is basically based on the appearance of a thing, person, or scene.

examples.jp: 今にも雨が降りそうです。／もうすぐ桜が咲きそうです。
examples.en: It looks like it will rain at any moment. / The cherry blossoms may soon be in bloom.

43.summary: Vます-stem／い-adj／な-adj + そうです bases a supposition purely on how something looks — its appearance, right now, before anything has actually happened.
43.details:
See **Lesson 47-2**'s details table for the full comparison distinguishing this appearance-based そうです from the hearsay そうです (Lesson 47-1) and the inference-based ようです (Lesson 47-2).

今にも雨が**降りそうです**。 *(It looks like it will rain any moment — judging from the sky right now.)*
もうすぐ桜が**咲きそうです**。 *(The cherry blossoms look like they'll bloom soon.)*

43.title: Vます-form ＋ そうです
43.meaning: When the present state makes the speaker presuppose an occurrence, いまにも／もうすぐ／これから, etc., are added to refer to the time when the speaker thinks the occurrence will take place.
43.explanation: When the present state makes the speaker presuppose an occurrence, いまにも／もうすぐ／これから, etc., are added to refer to the time when the speaker thinks the occurrence will take place.

examples.jp: シャンプーがなくなりそうです。
examples.en: It looks like we are running out of shampoo.

43.summary: Vます-stem + そうです is often paired with time adverbs (いまにも／もうすぐ／これから) that specify when the speaker expects the presupposed occurrence to happen.
43.details:
シャンプーが**なくなりそうです**。 *(It looks like we're running out of shampoo.)*

Adding いまにも (any moment now), もうすぐ (soon), or これから (from now on) sharpens exactly when the speaker expects the visually-suggested event to occur — without such an adverb, the timing is left a bit vaguer, just "it looks like this is heading that way.

43.title: い-adj（〜い）／な-adj［な］＋ そうです
43.structure: い-adj（〜い）／な-adj［な］＋ そうです
43.meaning: Means something hasn't been confirmed as a fact, but looks so judging from appearance.
43.explanation: Means something hasn't been confirmed as a fact, but looks so judging from appearance. [Note] For describing others' feelings (うれしい、かなしい、さびしい, etc.), 〜そうです must be used, because you can only guess how other people feel.

examples.jp: この料理は辛そうです。／ミラーさんはうれしそうです。
examples.en: This dish looks spicy. / Mr. Miller looks happy.

43.summary: い-adj／な-adj + そうです means something hasn't been confirmed as fact, but appears that way — and for describing someone else's internal feelings, this pattern is required, since you can only guess at what another person feels.
43.details:
この料理は**辛そうです**。 *(This dish looks spicy.)*
ミラーさんは**うれしそうです**。 *(Mr. Miller looks happy.)*

> **Why this pattern is required for others' feelings**: Adjectives like うれしい、かなしい、さびしい describe an internal emotional state you can never directly observe in someone else — you can only judge from their outward appearance. That's precisely what appearance-based そうです is for, which is why 〜そうです (not the plain adjective) must be used when describing how someone *else* seems to feel (as opposed to your own feelings, which you can state directly: わたしはうれしいです).

43.title: Vて-form 来ます
43.meaning: Means "to go somewhere, do something, and come back".
43.explanation: Means "to go somewhere, do something, and come back". The place where the action happens is marked with で; exceptionally, から marks it when a thing is moved away from that place and the move itself is the purpose. Two further uses: N（place）へ行って来ます ("go somewhere and come back", the action there unspecified) and 出かけて来ます ("go out and come back", both place and action unspecified).

examples.jp: ちょっとたばこを買って来ます。／郵便局へ行って来ます。／ちょっと出かけて来ます。
examples.en: I'm just popping out to buy some cigarettes. / I'm going to the post office (and coming back). / I'm going out (and coming back soon).

43.summary: て-form + 来ます means 'to go somewhere, do something, and come back' — the place is marked with で, except when moving a thing away from that place is itself the purpose, in which case から is used.
43.details:
### て-form + 来ます: Go, Do, and Return

- ちょっとたばこを**買って来ます**。 *(I'm popping out to buy cigarettes and come back.)*
- 郵便局へ**行って来ます**。 *(I'm going to the post office [and coming back] — action at the place unspecified.)*
- ちょっと**出かけて来ます**。 *(I'm going out and coming back soon — both place and action unspecified.)*

The place where the action itself happens is marked with で (コンビニでたばこを買って来ます); exceptionally, から marks the place when something is being moved *away from* it and that removal is the whole point (図書館から本を借りて来ます — "borrow a book from the library and bring it back").

44.title: Vます-form／い-adj（〜い）／な-adj［な］＋ すぎます
44.structure: Vます-form／い-adj（〜い）／な-adj［な］＋ すぎます
44.meaning: 〜すぎます indicates that the degree of an action or state is excessive.
44.explanation: 〜すぎます indicates that the degree of an action or state is excessive. It's therefore usually used with reference to undesirable states. 〜すぎます is classified as a Group II verb and conjugates the same way: のみすぎる、のみすぎ（ない）、のみすぎて.

examples.jp: ゆうべお酒を飲みすぎました。／このセーターは大きすぎます。
examples.en: I drank too much last night. / This sweater is too large (for me).

44.summary: すぎます says the degree of an action or state is excessive — almost always framing it as undesirable — and conjugates just like a Group II verb.
44.details:
ゆうべお酒を**飲みすぎました**。 *(I drank too much last night.)*
このセーターは**大きすぎます**。 *(This sweater is too big.)*

すぎます attaches to a Vます-stem, an い-adjective (drop い), or a な-adjective (drop な), and behaves as its own Group II verb from there: のみすぎる (dictionary form), のみすぎない (negative), のみすぎて (て-form). Because it inherently frames something as *excessive*, it's almost always used about undesirable states — you wouldn't usually say 上手すぎます to praise someone, for instance.

44.title: Vます-form ＋ やすいです／にくいです
44.structure: Vます-form ＋ やすいです／にくいです
44.meaning: These phrases depict the ease or difficulty of handling or doing something, or the ease/difficulty in the characteristics of an object or person changing, or of something happening.
44.explanation: These phrases depict the ease or difficulty of handling or doing something, or the ease/difficulty in the characteristics of an object or person changing, or of something happening. [Note] 〜やすい and 〜にくい function as い-adjectives and conjugate the same way as other い-adjectives.

examples.jp: このパソコンは使いやすいです。／白いシャツは汚れやすいです。
examples.en: This personal computer is easy to use. / A white shirt gets dirty easily.

44.summary: やすいです／にくいです describe how easy or hard something is to do, to handle, or for a change/event to occur — and both function grammatically as ordinary い-adjectives once attached.
44.details:
このパソコンは**使いやすいです**。 *(This computer is easy to use.)*
白いシャツは**汚れやすいです**。 *(A white shirt gets dirty easily.)*

Both やすい and にくい attach to a Vます-stem and then conjugate exactly like any other い-adjective: 使いやすかったです (past), 使いやすくないです (negative), 使いやすければ (conditional). They apply broadly — to the ease/difficulty of *doing* something (使いやすい, "easy to use"), or to how easily a characteristic *changes* (汚れやすい, "gets dirty easily").

44.title: い-adj（〜い→く）／な-adj［な→に］／N ＋ に します
44.structure: い-adj（〜い→く）／な-adj［な→に］／N ＋ に します
44.meaning: While 〜く／に なります (Lesson 19) indicates that something "turns into" a certain state on its own, 〜く／に します indicates that somebody deliberately "turns something into" a certain state.
44.explanation: While 〜く／に なります (Lesson 19) indicates that something "turns into" a certain state on its own, 〜く／に します indicates that somebody deliberately "turns something into" a certain state.

examples.jp: 音を大きくします。／部屋をきれいにします。
examples.en: I will turn up the volume. / I will clean my room.

44.summary: くします／にします means someone deliberately changes something into a state — the transitive counterpart to くなります／になります (Lesson 19), which describes something changing on its own.
44.details:
### くします／にします vs くなります／になります (L19)

| Pattern | Who/what changes it | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| い-adj／な-adj ＋ くなります／になります (L19) | Happens on its own, no deliberate agent | 部屋が**きれいになりました**。 *(The room became clean — on its own, or unstated.)* |
| **い-adj／な-adj ＋ くします／にします** (here) | Someone deliberately makes it happen | 部屋を**きれいにします**。 *(I will clean the room — a deliberate action.)* |

The same distinction shows up with が (intransitive/spontaneous) vs を (transitive/deliberate): 音が大きくなります (the volume goes up, by itself) vs 音を大きくします (I turn up the volume, deliberately).

44.title: Nに します
44.meaning: Nに します expresses selection and/or decision.
44.explanation: Nに します expresses selection and/or decision.

examples.jp: 部屋はシングルにしますか、ツインにしますか。
examples.en: Would you like a single room or a twin room?

44.summary: Nにします expresses a selection or decision — choosing one option among others.
44.details:
部屋はシングル**にしますか**、ツイン**にしますか**。
*(Would you like a single room or a twin room?)*

This is a distinct use of にします from Lesson 44-3's "change something into a state" — here N + にします simply means "I decide on/choose N," used constantly in ordering food, choosing options, and making selections: わたしはコーヒーにします (I'll have coffee — i.e., "I choose/decide on coffee").

44.title: い-adj（〜い→く）／な-adj［な→に］＋ V
44.meaning: When changing adjectives into the forms shown above, they function as adverbs.
44.explanation: When changing adjectives into the forms shown above, they function as adverbs.

examples.jp: 野菜を細かく切ってください。／電気や水は大切に使いましょう。
examples.en: Please cut the vegetables into small pieces. / Let's conserve electricity and water.

44.summary: い-adj くく／な-adj に turns the adjective into an adverb modifying the following verb.
44.details:
野菜を**細かく**切ってください。 *(Please cut the vegetables into small pieces.)*
電気や水は**大切に**使いましょう。 *(Let's use electricity and water carefully.)*

This is the same く／に conversion used in Lessons 19 and 44-3 (adjective-to-adverb via く for い-adjectives, に for な-adjectives) — here it modifies a verb describing *how* an action is done, rather than describing a change of state.

45.title: V dictionary form／V た-form／V ない-form ない／い-adj（〜い）／な-adj な／Nの ＋ 場合は、〜
45.structure: V dictionary form／V た-form／V ない-form ない／い-adj（〜い）／な-adj な／Nの ＋ 場合は、〜
45.meaning: 〜ばあいは is used to talk about a hypothetical situation.
45.explanation: 〜ばあいは is used to talk about a hypothetical situation. The sentence after it indicates how to cope with that situation or its consequence. Because 場合 is a noun, the forms of verbs, い-adjectives, な-adjectives, and nouns connected to it are the same as the forms used when modifying nouns.

examples.jp: 会議に間に合わない場合は、連絡してください。／領収書が必要な場合は、係に言ってください。
examples.en: If you cannot be in time for the meeting, please inform us. / When you need a receipt, please tell the person in charge.

45.summary: 場合は introduces a hypothetical situation, followed by how to cope with it — because 場合 is a noun, verbs/adjectives/nouns attach to it using the same noun-modifying forms you already use before any other noun.
45.details:
会議に間に合わない**場合は**、連絡してください。 *(If you can't make it to the meeting, please let us know.)*
領収書が必要**な場合は**、係に言ってください。 *(If you need a receipt, please tell the person in charge.)*

Because 場合 (situation/case) is grammatically an ordinary noun, everything before it takes the same form you'd use to modify any noun: dictionary form, た-form, ない-form ない, い-adjective plain, or な-adjective + な. 場合は tends to describe a more formal/procedural hypothetical (what to do "in the case that...") compared to conversational conditionals like たら or ば.

45.title: V／い-adj／な-adj plain form／N（だ→な）＋ のに、〜
45.structure: V／い-adj／な-adj plain form／N（だ→な）＋ のに、〜
45.meaning: のに is used when what's stated in the second clause runs contrary to what's expected from the first.
45.explanation: のに is used when what's stated in the second clause runs contrary to what's expected from the first. Unlike 〜が／〜ても, 〜のに can only refer to things that have actually occurred in reality (not a hypothetical possibility), and it strongly implies the speaker's unexpectedness or dissatisfaction — sometimes a reproach.

examples.jp: 約束をしたのに、彼女は来ませんでした。／きょうは日曜日なのに、働かなければなりません。
examples.en: She did not come, even though she promised. / Even though today is Sunday, I have to work.

45.summary: のに links two clauses where the second runs contrary to what the first would lead you to expect — unlike が／ても, this pattern only applies to things that actually happened, and it strongly conveys the speaker's surprise or dissatisfaction.
45.details:
### のに vs が／ても

| Pattern | Applies to | Nuance |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **のに** (here) | Only real, actually-occurred situations | Strong sense of unexpectedness, disappointment, or reproach |
| が／ても | Real or hypothetical situations | More neutral, no particular emotional charge |

約束をした**のに**、彼女は来ませんでした。 *(She didn't come, even though she'd promised — implying frustration/disappointment.)*
きょうは日曜日な**のに**、働かなければなりません。 *(Even though today is Sunday, I have to work — implying "that's not fair.")*

Because のに always signals the speaker's emotional reaction to a real contradiction, it can sound like a complaint or reproach even when that's not fully intended — worth being mindful of tone when using it.

46.title: V dictionary form／Vて-form いる／Vた-form ＋ ところです
46.structure: V dictionary form／Vて-form いる／Vた-form ＋ ところです
46.meaning: ところ originally means "place", but here indicates a temporal position — a certain point in time during the course of an action.
46.explanation: ところ originally means "place", but here indicates a temporal position — a certain point in time during the course of an action. Dictionary form + ところです shows a person is about to start something (often with これから／［ちょうど］いまから); て-form いる + ところです shows an action is currently underway (often with いま); た-form + ところです shows an action has just been completed (often with たったいま).

examples.jp: これから食べるところです。／今調べているところです。／たった今バスが出たところです。
examples.en: I'm just about to eat. / I am investigating it now. / The bus left just now.

46.summary: ところ ('place') is repurposed here to mark a point in time within an action's progress — about to start, currently underway, or just completed, depending on which verb form precedes it.
46.details:
### ところです: Three Points in an Action's Timeline

| Form | Timing | Typical adverb | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **V dictionary form ＋ ところです** | About to start | これから／［ちょうど］いまから | **これから食べるところです**。 *(I'm just about to eat.)* |
| **Vて-form いる ＋ ところです** | Currently underway | いま | **今調べているところです**。 *(I am investigating it right now.)* |
| **Vた-form ＋ ところです** | Just completed | たったいま | **たった今バスが出たところです**。 *(The bus left just now.)* |

See Lesson 46-2 (ばかりです) for a related but distinct pattern about recency.

46.title: Vた-form ＋ ばかりです
46.meaning: Means that not much time has passed since a certain action or event occurred.
46.explanation: Means that not much time has passed since a certain action or event occurred. It's an expression of the speaker's own feeling and can be used regardless of the real length of time that has passed, if the speaker feels it's short — unlike Vた-formところです, which can only indicate a moment right at completion.

examples.jp: さっき昼ごはんを食べたばかりです。／木村さんは先月この会社に入ったばかりです。
examples.en: I had lunch only a while ago. / Ms. Kimura joined this company only a month ago.

46.summary: ばかりです means not much time has passed since something happened — a subjective feeling of the speaker's, usable regardless of the actual elapsed time, unlike Vた-formところです, which can only mark the exact moment of completion.
46.details:
### ばかりです vs たところです

| Pattern | Nature | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Vた-form ＋ ばかりです** (here) | Subjective — "feels recent to me," regardless of the literal time elapsed | 木村さんは先月この会社に**入ったばかりです**。 *(Ms. Kimura joined only a month ago — still feels recent.)* |
| Vた-form ＋ ところです (L46-1) | Objective — right at the moment of completion | たった今バスが出た**ところです**。 *(The bus just left — this instant.)* |

さっき昼ごはんを食べたばかりです can be said even a couple of hours later if the speaker still feels it was "just now" — ところです couldn't stretch that way, since it marks the literal instant of completion.

46.title: V dictionary form／V ない-form ない／い-adj（〜い）／な-adj な／Nの ＋ はずです
46.structure: V dictionary form／V ない-form ない／い-adj（〜い）／な-adj な／Nの ＋ はずです
46.meaning: The speaker uses this pattern to show he/she is convinced of what's stated before はずです.
46.explanation: The speaker uses this pattern to show he/she is convinced of what's stated before はずです. By using this pattern, the speaker implies that he/she has grounds to think so, that it's his/her own judgment, and that he/she is quite sure of it.

examples.jp: ミラーさんはきょう来るはずですよ。きのう電話がありましたから。
examples.en: I'm sure Mr. Miller will come today. I received a phone call from him yesterday.

46.summary: はずです shows the speaker is convinced of something, based on their own grounds/evidence, and states it with real confidence — distinct from a weaker guess like かもしれません or でしょう.
46.details:
ミラーさんはきょう来る**はずです**よ。きのう電話がありましたから。
*(I'm sure Mr. Miller will come today — I got a call from him yesterday [so I have grounds to be confident].)*

はずです always implies the speaker has a concrete reason for their conviction (here, "he called yesterday [and said he'd come]") — it's stronger than でしょう (plain inference) and much stronger than かもしれません (low-certainty possibility). If evidence later contradicts a はずです statement, it typically triggers surprise: おかしいですね。来るはずなんですが… ("That's odd — he was supposed to come...").

47.title: plain form ＋ そうです
47.meaning: "I hear that..." — an expression for conveying information you've obtained from another source without adding your own point of view.
47.explanation: "I hear that..." — an expression for conveying information you've obtained from another source without adding your own point of view. When the source is given, it's indicated by 〜によると ("according to ~") at the start of the sentence. [Note] This is different in meaning and construction from the appearance-based 〜そうです in Lesson 43 (雨が降りそうです "it looks like rain" vs 雨が降るそうです "I hear it will rain").

examples.jp: 天気予報によると、あしたは寒くなるそうです。
examples.en: According to the weather forecast, it will be cold tomorrow.

47.summary: plain form + そうです (hearsay) conveys information from another source, without adding the speaker's own judgment — grammatically and semantically distinct from the appearance-based そうです in Lesson 43.
47.details:
See **Lesson 47-2**'s details table for the full 3-way comparison of hearsay-そうです (here), appearance-そうです (L43), and inference-ようです (L47-2).

天気予報**によると**、あしたは寒くなる**そうです**。
*(According to the weather forecast, it will be cold tomorrow.)*

When the source is worth naming, 〜によると ("according to ~") opens the sentence. Note the connecting form: hearsay そうです attaches to the full plain form (寒くなる**そうです**), while appearance そうです attaches to the ます-stem or adjective stem (寒**そうです**) — a small but telling structural difference that signals which meaning is intended.

47.title: V／い-adj／な-adj plain form（だ→な）／N plain form（だ→の） ＋ ようです
47.structure: V／い-adj／な-adj plain form（だ→な）／N plain form（だ→の） ＋ ようです
47.meaning: 〜ようです conveys the speaker's subjective conjecture, based on information obtained through his/her own senses — sometimes accompanied by どうも, which suggests the speaker can't be fully certain.
47.explanation: 〜ようです conveys the speaker's subjective conjecture, based on information obtained through his/her own senses — sometimes accompanied by どうも, which suggests the speaker can't be fully certain. [Note] Compared with 〜そうです (Lesson 43, an intuitive, appearance-based judgment): 忙しそうです is based on how Mr. Miller looks right now, while 忙しいようです is based on more evidence — what the speaker has seen, heard, or been told.

examples.jp: 人が大勢集まっていますね。事故のようですね。パトカーと救急車が来ていますよ。
examples.en: Look, there is a big crowd. It looks like there's been an accident. A patrol car and an ambulance are there.

47.summary: そうです (appearance), そうです (hearsay), and ようです (inference) all guess or report something not directly confirmed, but differ in what evidence they're based on.
47.details:
### Comparing 〜そうです and 〜ようです

Minna no Nihongo introduces three different-looking but easily confused patterns across Lessons 43 and 47. They all describe something the speaker is not 100% sure of, but the basis for the guess is different in each case.

| Pattern | Connects to | Based on... | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **〜そうです** (appearance, L43) | Vます-stem／い-adj（〜い）／な-adj［な］ | A visual impression, right now, before anything has happened | 今にも雨が**降りそうです**。 *(It looks like it's about to rain — judging by the sky right now.)* |
| **〜そうです** (hearsay, L47) | plain form | Something the speaker heard or read — no personal judgment added | 天気予報によると、あした雨が**降るそうです**。 *(I hear it's going to rain tomorrow — according to the forecast.)* |
| **〜ようです** (inference, L47) | V／い-adj／な-adj plain form（だ→な）／N plain form（だ→の） | The speaker's own reasoning from several pieces of evidence (what they've seen, heard, or pieced together) | 空が暗いし、風も強いし、雨が**降るようです**。 *(It looks like it's going to rain — the sky is dark, the wind is strong, and so on.)* |

> **Key distinction**: 忙しそうです describes how someone looks *right now*; 忙しいようです is a conclusion the speaker has reached from more accumulated evidence (what was seen, heard, or told). 雨が降るそうです is purely secondhand — it carries no visual or logical judgment of the speaker's own at all.

47.title: 声／音／におい／味 が します
47.structure: 声／音／におい／味 が します
47.meaning: A phenomenon that's perceivable by the senses is described using 〜がします.
47.explanation: A phenomenon that's perceivable by the senses is described using 〜がします. こえがします、においがします、あじがします all mean that these things have been perceived or sensed, regardless of the speaker's intention.

examples.jp: 変な音がしますね。
examples.en: There's a strange sound, isn't there?

47.summary: 声／音／におい／味が します describes something perceived through the senses — hearing, smelling, or tasting something, regardless of anyone's intention.
47.details:
変な**音がします**ね。 *(There's a strange sound, isn't there?)*

こえがします (a voice is heard), においがします (a smell is noticed), あじがします (a taste is perceived) all describe a sensory experience that simply happens to the observer — nobody is deliberately making the sound/smell/taste, and nobody is deliberately perceiving it either; it's just there to be sensed. This parallels 見えます／聞こえます (Lesson 27-3) as another example of spontaneous, non-volitional sensory perception in Japanese.

48.title: Causative Verbs
48.structure: Group I: -u→-a＋せる／Group II: ＋させる／Group III: 来る→来させる、する→させる
48.meaning: Expresses making or letting someone do something — used to indicate compulsion (forcing a junior to act) or permission (allowing someone to act).
48.explanation: All causative verbs are Group II verbs and conjugate into the dictionary form, ない-form, て-form, etc. Group I: change the ます-stem to the あ-line and add せます (いきます→いかせます). Group II: drop ます and add させます (たべます→たべさせます). Group III: きます→こさせます, します→させます.

examples.jp: いかせる、いかせ（ない）、いかせて
examples.en: make/let go, (not) make/let go, making/letting go

48.summary: Causative verbs express 'make/let someone do'. Used mainly by a senior toward a junior (parent–child, boss–employee) to show compulsion or permission. All causative verbs conjugate as Group II verbs.
48.details:
### Causative Verb Conjugation (使役形の作り方) All causative verbs express "make/let someone do" and conjugate as **Group II verbs** (dictionary form ends in `-る`). | Verb Group | Conjugation Rule | Dictionary / Polite Form | Causative Form | Meaning | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Group I (五段)** | Final `-u` sound → `-a sound + せる`
(`-imasu` → `-asemasu`) | 行く (いきます)
飲む (のみます)
待つ (まちます)
手伝う (てつだいます) | **行かせる** (いかせます)
**飲ませる** (のませます)
**待たせる** (またせます)
**手伝わせる** (てつだわせます) | Make/let go
Make/let drink
Make/let wait
Make/let help | | **Group II (一段)** | Drop `-る` → `+ させる`
(ます-stem `+ させ・ます`) | 食べる (たべます)
やめる (やめます) | **食べさせる** (たべさせます)
**やめさせる** (やめさせます) | Make/let eat
Make/let quit | | **Group III (不規則)** | Irregular | 来る (きます)
する (します) | **来させる** (こさせます)
**させる** (させます) | Make/let come
Make/let do | --- ### Core Sentence Patterns 1. **Intransitive verb (N（person）を V-causative)**: - 部長は加藤さんを大阪へ出張**させます**。 *(The manager sends Mr. Kato to Osaka on business.)* - When the intransitive verb's sentence also names a place with を (e.g. 自由に遊ばせる), the person doing the action is marked with に instead. 2. **Transitive verb (N（person）に N（object）を V-causative)**: - 娘に朝ごはんの準備を手伝わ**せます**。 *(I have my daughter help prepare breakfast.)* 3. **Requesting permission (V-causative て-form ＋ いただけませんか)**: - 早退させ**ていただけませんか**。 *(Would you let me leave work early?)* > **Compulsion vs. Permission**: Whether a causative sentence means "make" (force) or "let" (allow) depends entirely on context — 娘を遊ばせました can mean either "I made my daughter play" or "I let my daughter play," depending on the situation.

48.title: N（person）を V（intransitive）causative
48.explanation: "Make/let a person do V (intransitive verb)". [Note] When an intransitive verb is used with "N（place）を" in the sentence, the subject of the action is marked with に instead; without a を-phrase, the subject is marked with を.

examples.jp: 部長は加藤さんを大阪へ出張させます。／わたしは娘を自由に遊ばせました。
examples.en: The department manager makes Mr. Kato go to Osaka on business. / I let my daughter play freely.

48.summary: 'Make/let a person do V' with an intransitive verb — whether the person is marked with を or に depends on whether the sentence also names a place with を.
48.details:
部長は加藤さんを大阪へ**出張させます**。 *(The manager sends Mr. Kato to Osaka on business.)*
わたしは娘を自由に**遊ばせました**。 *(I let my daughter play freely.)*

> **を vs に for the causee**: When the sentence also has a "N（place）を" phrase (e.g. 公園**を**歩かせる, "make [someone] walk through the park"), the person doing the action is marked with **に** instead, since を is already taken by the place. Without a を-phrase, the person is marked with **を**, as in the examples above.

48.title: N（person）に N を V（transitive）causative

examples.jp: 朝は忙しいですから、娘に朝ごはんの準備を手伝わせます。
examples.en: I am busy in the morning, so I make my daughter help prepare breakfast.

48.summary: 'Make/let a person do V' with a transitive verb — the person doing the action is marked with に, and the object of that action keeps を, exactly like the passive construction's N1にN2をVpassive shape.
48.details:
朝は忙しいですから、娘**に**朝ごはんの準備**を**手伝わせます。
*(I am busy in the morning, so I make my daughter help prepare breakfast.)*

Compare the pattern shape N（person）に N（object）を V-causative with the passive's N1（人）はN2（人）にN3をVpassive (Lesson 37-3) — both use に for the "other person" involved and を for the object, even though causative and passive express opposite relationships (making someone act, vs. being affected by someone's act).

48.title: Usage of the causative
48.meaning: Causative verbs indicate compulsion or permission.
48.explanation: Causative verbs indicate compulsion or permission. A causative sentence is used when the relationship between a senior and a junior person is clear (parent/child, senior/junior colleague, superior/subordinate) and the senior person forces the junior person to do something, or allows him/her to. When the speaker talks about someone from within his own group to a person outside it, the causative is used regardless of their relative status. [Note] When a junior speaks of a senior doing something for them, Vて-formいただきます is used (or Vて-formもらいます if their relationship is more equal/ambiguous) — a causative sentence is not normally used to describe a senior person doing something for a junior, except with verbs of emotion (あんしんする、しんぱいする、がっかりする、よろこぶ、かなしむ、おこる, etc.).

examples.jp: 駅に着いたら、お電話ください。係の者を迎えに行かせますから。／子どものとき、体が弱くて、母を心配させました。
examples.en: When you arrive at the station, please call me. I will send a member of my staff to pick you up. / When I was a child, my poor health worried my mother.

48.summary: Causative sentences are used when a clear senior-junior relationship lets one person compel or permit the other — with a key exception for verbs of emotion, and a reminder that a junior speaking of a senior's action for them uses ていただきます instead.
48.details:
### When Causative Sentences Are (and Aren't) Used

- Used when relative status is clear: parent/child, senior/junior colleague, boss/subordinate — the senior forces or allows the junior to act.
- Also used regardless of relative status when the speaker talks about someone from *within their own group* (ウチ) to an outsider (ソト).
- **Exception — verbs of emotion**: causative can describe a senior doing something *for* a junior when the verb expresses causing an emotional reaction (あんしんさせる、しんぱいさせる、がっかりさせる、よろこばせる、かなしませる、おこらせる): 子どものとき、体が弱くて、母を**心配させました**。 *(My poor health worried my mother, when I was a child.)*
- **What NOT to use for the reverse direction**: A junior describing a senior doing something *for them* uses Vて-form いただきます (or もらいます if the relationship is more equal/ambiguous) — not the causative, except for the emotion-verb exception above.

48.title: V causative て-form いただけませんか
48.structure: V causative て-form いただけませんか
48.meaning: Used to seek permission — different from Vて-formいただけませんか (Lesson 26), which is used to request someone to do something.
48.explanation: Used to seek permission — different from Vて-formいただけませんか (Lesson 26), which is used to request someone to do something. In おしえていただけませんか, the listener will do the teaching; in そうたいさせていただけませんか, the speaker will do the leaving early.

examples.jp: 友達の結婚式があるので、早退させていただけませんか。
examples.en: As I'm going to attend my friend's wedding, would you please let me leave earlier?

48.summary: V causative て-form + いただけませんか is used to seek permission for the speaker's own action — different from the plain て-form ＋ いただけませんか (Lesson 26), which requests that the listener do something.
48.details:
### Requesting Permission vs. Requesting an Action

| Pattern | Who acts | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Vて-form ＋ いただけませんか (L26) | The **listener** | 紹介**していただけませんか**。 *(Would you introduce [someone] to me?)* |
| **V causative て-form ＋ いただけませんか** (here) | The **speaker** (seeking permission to act) | 早退**させていただけませんか**。 *(Would you let me leave early?)* |

友達の結婚式があるので、**早退させていただけませんか**。 *(As I'm attending my friend's wedding, would you please let me leave work early?)* — the causative て-form (させて) is what shifts the meaning from "please do X for me" to "please let me do X.

49.title: 敬語 (けいご) — overview
49.meaning: けいご are expressions showing the speaker's respect, depending on his/her relationship with the listener or the person being referred to: (1) whether the speaker is junior or lower in social status, (2) whether the speaker and listener have a close acquaintanceship, and (3) the ウチ・ソト relationship — the speaker's own group (family, company) is ウチ ("in"), everyone else is ソト ("out"), and an insider is never elevated with けいご when talking to an outsider, however senior that insider is within the group.
49.explanation: けいご are expressions showing the speaker's respect, depending on his/her relationship with the listener or the person being referred to: (1) whether the speaker is junior or lower in social status, (2) whether the speaker and listener have a close acquaintanceship, and (3) the ウチ・ソト relationship — the speaker's own group (family, company) is ウチ ("in"), everyone else is ソト ("out"), and an insider is never elevated with けいご when talking to an outsider, however senior that insider is within the group. けいご has three types: そんけいご (respectful expressions, this lesson), けんじょうご (humble expressions, Lesson 50), and ていねいご (polite expressions, Lesson 50).

examples.jp: そんけいご describes the listener or the person referred to, and their actions.
examples.en: Respectful expressions are used for the listener/referent and their actions — never for the speaker's own.

49.summary: Respectful language (尊敬語) elevates the actions of the listener or superior. Uses special honorific verbs or お〜になります.
49.details:
### Respectful Keigo (尊敬語) Summary Table

Used exclusively for the actions of superiors, customers, or business partners.

| Plain / Polite Verb | Special Respectful Verb (尊敬語) | Regular Form (`お + stem + になります`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 行きます / 来ます / います | **いらっしゃいます** / **おいでになります** | — |
| 食べます / 飲みます | **召し上がります** (めしあがります) | — |
| 言います | **おっしゃいます** | — |
| 知っています | **ご存じです** (ごぞんじです) | — |
| 見ます | **ご覧になります** (ごらんになります) | — |
| します | **なさいます** | — |
| くれます | **くださいます** | — |
| 書きます | — | **お書きになります** |
| 読みます | — | **お読みになります** |
| 帰ります | — | **お帰りになります** |

49.title: Respectful verbs — Group II conjugation (れる/られる)
49.structure: Respectful verbs — Group II conjugation (れる/られる)
49.meaning: The same verb forms used in the passive voice are also used as respectful verbs; they're all Group II verbs.
49.explanation: The same verb forms used in the passive voice are also used as respectful verbs; they're all Group II verbs.

examples.jp: 中村さんは7時に来られます。／お酒をやめられたんですか。
examples.en: Mr. Nakamura is coming at seven. / Have you given up drinking?

49.summary: The same れる／られる forms used for the passive voice double as a respectful verb form — all conjugating as Group II verbs, just like their passive counterparts.
49.details:
中村さんは7時に**来られます**。 *(Mr. Nakamura is coming at seven — respectful, not passive, here.)*
お酒を**やめられた**んですか。 *(Have you given up drinking? — respectful.)*

Context (a person of higher status as the subject, no sense of "being affected") signals the respectful reading rather than the passive one — 来られる could mean either "is respectfully coming" or "[I am inconvenienced by] someone coming," and only context disambiguates. This form is considered a notch less formal than the special respectful words (49-4) or the お～になります pattern (49-3).

49.title: お V ます-form に なります
49.structure: お V ます-form に なります
49.meaning: This pattern is considered more polite than the respectful れる／られる form above.
49.explanation: This pattern is considered more polite than the respectful れる／られる form above. It's not applicable to verbs whose ます-form consists of one mora, like みます or ねます — for those, and for verbs with special respectful equivalents, the special word is used instead.

examples.jp: 社長はもうお帰りになりました。
examples.en: The president has already left for home.

49.summary: お + ます-stem + になります is considered more polite than the れる／られる respectful form, but doesn't apply to one-mora ます-stems or to verbs that already have a dedicated special respectful word.
49.details:
社長はもう**お帰りになりました**。 *(The president has already gone home.)*

> **Restrictions**: Not used for verbs whose ます-stem is a single mora (見ます, 寝ます — for these, special words or れる／られる are used instead), and not used for verbs that already have a special respectful equivalent (see Lesson 49-4) — for those, the special word always takes priority over building お～になります.

49.title: Special respectful words
49.meaning: Some verbs have entirely separate respectful equivalents, considered to show the same level of respect as お Vます-formになります: いらっしゃいます (be／go／come), めしあがります (eat／drink), くださいます (give), おっしゃいます (say), なさいます (do), ごらんになります (see／look at), ごぞんじです (know).
49.explanation: Some verbs have entirely separate respectful equivalents, considered to show the same level of respect as お Vます-formになります: いらっしゃいます (be／go／come), めしあがります (eat／drink), くださいます (give), おっしゃいます (say), なさいます (do), ごらんになります (see／look at), ごぞんじです (know). [Note] いらっしゃいます、なさいます、くださいます、and おっしゃいます are Group I verbs, but conjugate irregularly outside the ます-form (changing in the ら-row).

examples.jp: ワット先生は研究室にいらっしゃいます。／どうぞ召し上がってください。
examples.en: Professor Watt is in the office. / Please help yourselves.

49.summary: Some verbs have entirely separate respectful words rather than a derived form — considered equally polite to お～になります, but with some irregular Group I conjugation to watch for.
49.details:
### Special Respectful Verbs

| Plain/Polite | Respectful |
| :--- | :--- |
| います／行きます／来ます | **いらっしゃいます** |
| 食べます／飲みます | **召し上がります** |
| くれます | **くださいます** |
| 言います | **おっしゃいます** |
| します | **なさいます** |
| 見ます | **ご覧になります** |
| 知っています | **ご存じです** |

ワット先生は研究室に**いらっしゃいます**。 *(Professor Watt is in his office.)* どうぞ**召し上がって**ください。 *(Please help yourself.)*

> **Irregular conjugation**: いらっしゃいます、なさいます、くださいます、おっしゃいます are Group I verbs, but conjugate irregularly outside the ます-form — they change in the ら-row rather than following the expected pattern (e.g. いらっしゃる → the ます-form is いらっしゃい**ます**, not the expected いらっしゃり**ます**).

49.title: お V ます-form ください
49.structure: お V ます-form ください
49.meaning: The respectful way of instructing or inviting someone to do something.
49.explanation: The respectful way of instructing or inviting someone to do something. [Note] The special respectful words above cannot be used in this pattern — めしあがります and ごらんになります change instead to おめしあがりください and ごらんください.

examples.jp: あちらからお入りください。
examples.en: Please enter from over there.

49.summary: お + ます-stem + ください is the respectful way to instruct or invite someone to do something — special respectful words plug into a slightly different shape here instead of the regular お～ください pattern.
49.details:
あちらから**お入りください**。 *(Please enter from over there.)*

> **Exception for special respectful words**: The special words from Lesson 49-4 can't slot into this pattern in their usual form — 召し上がります and ご覧になります instead become **お召し上がりください** and **ご覧ください** respectively, keeping the overall お／ご＋ください shape rather than literally inserting the special verb's stem.

49.title: お／ご + noun, adjective, adverb
49.meaning: Nouns, adjectives, and adverbs can also be turned into そんけいご by attaching お or ご to the front.
49.explanation: Nouns, adjectives, and adverbs can also be turned into そんけいご by attaching お or ご to the front. お is generally attached to words of Japanese origin (お名前, お元気, お忙しい, ご自由に); ご to words of Chinese origin (ご家族, ご意見, ご旅行, ご熱心, ご親切).

examples.jp: お名前／ご住所
examples.en: (your) name / (your) address

49.summary: お or ご attached to a noun, adjective, or adverb turns it into そんけいご — お for native Japanese-origin words, ご for Chinese-origin (漢語) words, as a general rule of thumb.
49.details:
### お vs ご: Which Prefix Goes Where

| Prefix | Typically attaches to | Examples |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **お** | Native Japanese-origin (和語) words | お名前、お元気、お忙しい、ご自由に (exception) |
| **ご** | Chinese-origin (漢語) words | ご家族、ご意見、ご旅行、ご熱心、ご親切 |

This origin-based rule (native → お, Chinese-derived → ご) is a helpful general guideline, but there are exceptions worth just memorizing as you encounter them (ご自由に uses ご despite じゆう being a native-feeling reading) — when in doubt, learn the specific word's convention rather than relying purely on the rule.

49.title: Keigo, sentence style, and consistency
49.meaning: A sentence can end with a plain form of けいご on occasions when the speaker is talking to a close friend about a person to whom he/she wishes to show respect.
49.explanation: A sentence can end with a plain form of けいご on occasions when the speaker is talking to a close friend about a person to whom he/she wishes to show respect. But replacing just a single word with けいご isn't enough — a uniform level of けいご must be kept throughout the whole sentence: おくさま and いっしょ become ごいっしょ to stay consistent with a respectful verb like いかれます. When you want to be very polite, Vて-formまして replaces Vて-form, often for the same reason of overall consistency.

examples.jp: 部長の奥様もごいっしょにゴルフに行かれます。／ハンスがゆうべ熱を出しまして、けさもまだ下がらないんです。
examples.en: The general manager's wife will go golfing together with him. / Hans became feverish last night and he still has a fever this morning.

49.summary: Keigo must be used consistently across a whole sentence, not just on one word — and the more formal ましたform Vて-formまして sometimes replaces a plain て-form for the same reason of overall consistency.
49.details:
### Consistency Across a Keigo Sentence

部長の奥様も**ごいっしょに**ゴルフに**行かれます**。
*(The manager's wife will go golfing together with him.)*

Notice いっしょ became ごいっしょ specifically to match the respectful verb 行かれます later in the sentence — using plain いっしょ here, next to a respectful verb, would feel inconsistent. Likewise, Vて-formまして can replace a plain て-form for the same reason:

ハンスがゆうべ熱を**出しまして**、けさもまだ下がらないんです。
*(Hans developed a fever last night, and it still hasn't gone down this morning.)*

> **Rule of thumb**: a sentence can end in plain form when talking about a respected third person to a close friend, but every keigo-marked element within it should agree on the same overall level of politeness — mixing a highly respectful verb with a casually blunt noun (or vice versa) reads as inconsistent, even if each piece is individually "correct."

50.title: 謙譲語 (けんじょうご) — overview
50.structure: 謙譲語 (けんじょうご) — overview
50.meaning: けんじょうご are expressions in which the speaker humbles himself/herself and lowers his/her own acts, to show respect to the listener or the person being referred to — directed at a person of higher social status or ソトのひと (an outsider).
50.explanation: けんじょうご are expressions in which the speaker humbles himself/herself and lowers his/her own acts, to show respect to the listener or the person being referred to — directed at a person of higher social status or ソトのひと (an outsider). けんじょうご is also used when the speaker refers to ウチのひと (an insider) in front of an outsider.

examples.jp: お荷物、お持ちしましょうか。
examples.en: It looks heavy. Shall I carry it for you?

50.summary: Humble language (謙譲語) lowers the speaker's own actions out of respect for the listener. Uses special humble verbs or お〜します.
50.details:
### Humble Keigo (謙譲語) Summary Table

Used exclusively for the speaker's own actions when interacting with or doing something for a superior.

| Plain / Polite Verb | Special Humble Verb (謙譲語) | Regular Form (`お + stem + します`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 行きます / 来ます | **参ります** (まいります) | — |
| います | **おります** | — |
| 食べます / 飲みます / もらいます | **いただきます** | — |
| 言います | **申します** (もうします) / **申し上げます** | — |
| します | **いたします** | — |
| 見ます | **拝見します** (はいけんします) | — |
| 知りません / わかりません | **存じません** (ぞんじません) | — |
| 会います | **お目にかかります** | — |
| 聞きます / 訪問します | **伺います** (うかがいます) | — |
| 持ちます | — | **お持ちします** |
| 案内します | — | **ご案内します** |

50.title: お V(Group I／II) ます-form します／ご V(Group III) します
50.structure: お V(Group I／II) ます-form します／ご V(Group III) します
50.meaning: This pattern is used for acts that involve another person besides the agent of the act — it isn't applicable to an act that doesn't involve anyone else (e.g. 私は来月国へ帰ります cannot become お帰りします).
50.explanation: This pattern is used for acts that involve another person besides the agent of the act — it isn't applicable to an act that doesn't involve anyone else (e.g. 私は来月国へ帰ります cannot become お帰りします). Not applicable to verbs whose ます-form is one mora, like みます or います. ごVします applies to Group III verbs that imply some association with the listener, such as しょうかいします、そうだんします、れんらくします — but でんわします and やくそくします are exceptions, taking お instead of ご.

examples.jp: 私が社長にスケジュールをお知らせします。／江戸東京博物館へご案内します。
examples.en: I will tell the president the schedule. / I will take you to the Edo-Tokyo Museum.

50.summary: お + Group I／II ます-stem + します／ご + Group III + します is used only for acts that involve another person besides the doer — and a handful of Group III verbs use お instead of the expected ご.
50.details:
私が社長にスケジュールを**お知らせします**。 *(I will let the president know the schedule.)*
江戸東京博物館へ**ご案内します**。 *(I will take you to the Edo-Tokyo Museum.)*

> **Restrictions**:
> - Not usable for an act that doesn't involve anyone else — 私は来月国へ帰ります can't become お帰りします, since "going home" doesn't involve another person as its recipient.
> - Not usable for one-mora ます-stems (見ます, います) — special humble words are used instead (see Lesson 50-3).
> - ご＋します applies to Group III verbs implying association with the listener (しょうかいします → ご紹介します, そうだんします → ご相談します, れんらくします → ご連絡します) — but でんわします and やくそくします are exceptions, taking お instead: お電話します、お約束します。

50.title: Special humble verbs
50.meaning: Some verbs have entirely separate humble equivalents: まいります (go／come), おります (be), いただきます (eat／drink／receive), もうします (say), いたします (do), はいけんします (see), ぞんじます (know), うかがいます (ask／hear／visit), おめにかかります (meet).
50.explanation: Some verbs have entirely separate humble equivalents: まいります (go／come), おります (be), いただきます (eat／drink／receive), もうします (say), いたします (do), はいけんします (see), ぞんじます (know), うかがいます (ask／hear／visit), おめにかかります (meet). Some are used only when the speaker's act directly involves the listener or the person being referred to (伺います、おめにかかります); others are used simply as humble self-reference, without necessarily involving anyone else (まいります、もうします).

examples.jp: 社長の奥様にお目にかかりました。／ミラーと申します。／アメリカから参りました。
examples.en: I met the president's wife. / My name is Miller. / I come from the United States.

50.summary: Some verbs have entirely separate humble equivalents — some used only when the act directly involves the listener/referent, others used simply as humble self-reference regardless of who else is involved.
50.details:
### Special Humble Verbs, and Who They Involve

| Plain/Polite | Humble | Requires the listener/referent involved? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 会います | **お目にかかります** | Yes |
| 聞きます／訪問します | **伺います** | Yes |
| 行きます／来ます | **参ります** | No — pure self-reference |
| 言います | **申します** | No — pure self-reference |
| います | **おります** | No |
| します | **いたします** | No |
| 見ます | **拝見します** | Usually yes (viewing something of theirs) |
| 知りません | **存じません** | No |

社長の奥様に**お目にかかりました**。 *(I met the president's wife.)* — involves the listener/referent directly.
アメリカから**参りました**。 *(I come from the United States.)* — pure humble self-reference, no one else involved.

50.title: 丁寧語 (ていねいご) — polite expressions
50.structure: 丁寧語 (ていねいご) — polite expressions
50.meaning: ていねいご show the speaker's respect to the listener, independent of who's being talked about.
50.explanation: ていねいご show the speaker's respect to the listener, independent of who's being talked about. ございます is the polite equivalent of あります; 〜でございます is the polite equivalent of です; よろしいでしょうか is a polite equivalent of いいですか.

examples.jp: 電話は階段の横にございます。／はい、IMCでございます。／お飲み物は何がよろしいでしょうか。
examples.en: The pay phone is beside the stairs. / Hello, this is IMC. / What would you like to drink?

50.summary: 丁寧語 shows respect to the listener regardless of who's being talked about — distinct from そんけいご (elevates the other person) and けんじょうご (lowers the speaker), which both depend on who the sentence is about.
50.details:
### 丁寧語: Politeness to the Listener, Regardless of Topic

| Plain/Polite | 丁寧語 |
| :--- | :--- |
| あります | **ございます** |
| です | **でございます** |
| いいですか | **よろしいでしょうか** |

電話は階段の横に**ございます**。 *(The pay phone is beside the stairs.)*
はい、IMC**でございます**。 *(Hello, this is IMC.)*
お飲み物は何が**よろしいでしょうか**。 *(What would you like to drink?)*

Unlike そんけいご (Lesson 49, elevates the listener or the person being talked about) or けんじょうご (Lesson 50-1, humbles the speaker's own actions), 丁寧語 is topic-independent — it simply dresses up the sentence itself more formally, which is why it's the register you hear constantly in customer service and receptionist speech, regardless of what's being discussed.
